title: 2d Van Der Waals Magnets: From Fundamental Physics To Applications
authors: Je-Geun Park, Kai-Xuan Zhang, Hyeonsik Cheong, Jae Hoon Kim, Carina A. Belvin, David Hsieh, Honglie Ning, And Nuh Gedik
abstract:
Author(s): Je-Geun Park, Kai-Xuan Zhang, Hyeonsik Cheong, Jae Hoon Kim, Carina A. Belvin, David Hsieh, Honglie Ning, and Nuh Gedik

Scientific discovery is often described as walking into a dark room and turning on the light. The discovery of 2D magnetism in van der Waals materials in 2016 was one such leap forward, removing one spatial dimension from macroscopic materials. The study of 2D magnets has challenged established theories and uncovered new phenomena. This review summarizes the current state of knowledge of magnetic phenomena in 2D van der Waals materials. The field encompasses not just the traditional study of ferromagnets and antiferromagnets but also topology, quantum and nonequilibrium dynamics, Floquet effects, magnons and spintronics, and the interaction of magnetism with light, phonons, and electric fields (multiferroics). The field is actively evolving, expanding theoretical understanding, materials capabilities, and experimental phenomenology while opening new directions for application.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 98, 025003] Published Wed May 27, 2026.
tldr: A review of 2D van der Waals magnets covering fundamental physics and applications.
motivation: To summarize the current state of knowledge in 2D magnetism, which has seen rapid progress since 2016.
method: The paper is a review, synthesizing results from many experimental and theoretical studies.
result: It covers ferromagnets, antiferromagnets, topology, quantum dynamics, Floquet effects, magnons, spintronics, and multiferroics.
conclusion: The field is actively evolving and opening new directions for applications.

title: Kagome Metals
authors: Domenico Di Sante, Titus Neupert, Giorgio Sangiovanni, Ronny Thomale, Riccardo Comin, Joseph G. Checkelsky, Ilija Zeljkovic, And Stephen D. Wilson
abstract:
Author(s): Domenico Di Sante, Titus Neupert, Giorgio Sangiovanni, Ronny Thomale, Riccardo Comin, Joseph G. Checkelsky, Ilija Zeljkovic, and Stephen D. Wilson

The kagome lattice is a two-dimensional tiling of hexagons and triangles named after a Japanese basket weaving technique. Its geometry gives rise to highly frustrated interactions and interference effects experienced by electrons and their multiple degrees of freedom. In metals, the exploration of materials with kagome conduction networks is driven by predictions of realizing new electronic states where these interference effects are dominant, amplifying electronic interactions and many-body effects. In these kagome metals, these amplified correlation effects in combination with spin-orbit coupling and other forms of frustration have given rise to a wealth of phenomena beyond expectations. These include unusual states and responses born from topological flat bands, massive Dirac fermions, sublattice interference effects at saddle points such as unconventional superconductivity, orbital antiferromagnetism and flux phases, amplified anomalous Hall effects, and electronic nematic states. This review examines the theoretical and experimental work on kagome metals, with the aim of elucidating fundamental mechanisms underlying the observed exotic phenomena.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 98, 015002] Published Thu Feb 12, 2026.
tldr: A review of kagome metals, focusing on exotic electronic states arising from geometric frustration and interference effects.
motivation: To understand the fundamental mechanisms behind unusual phenomena in kagome metals, such as unconventional superconductivity and topological flat bands.
method: The paper reviews theoretical and experimental work on kagome metals, synthesizing findings from multiple studies.
result: Kagome metals exhibit a wealth of exotic phenomena including topological flat bands, massive Dirac fermions, unconventional superconductivity, and orbital antiferromagnetism.
conclusion: The kagome lattice provides a rich platform for exploring correlated electron physics and may lead to new quantum states.

title: Spin-glass Dynamics: Experiment, Theory, And Simulation
authors: E. D. Dahlberg, I. González-Adalid Pemartín, E. Marinari, G. Parisi, F. Ricci-Tersenghi, V. Martin-Mayor, J. Moreno-Gordo, R. L. Orbach, I. Paga, J. J. Ruiz-Lorenzo, And D. Yllanes
abstract:
Author(s): E. D. Dahlberg, I. González-Adalid Pemartín, E. Marinari, G. Parisi, F. Ricci-Tersenghi, V. Martin-Mayor, J. Moreno-Gordo, R. L. Orbach, I. Paga, J. J. Ruiz-Lorenzo, and D. Yllanes

This review updates the field of spin glasses with broad application to a large variety of physical systems. In particular, this review tracks the progress of experiment, theory, and large-scale simulations. It highlights the importance of their synergy, from the inception of the field to the present day, and includes future opportunities for research.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 045005] Published Mon Dec 15, 2025.
tldr: A review of spin-glass dynamics covering experiment, theory, and simulation, with broad applications to physical systems.
motivation: Spin glasses serve as a model system for complex disordered systems, and understanding their dynamics is relevant to many areas of physics.
method: The review synthesizes experimental results, theoretical developments, and large-scale numerical simulations to track progress in the field.
result: The paper highlights the synergy between experiment, theory, and simulation, and identifies future research opportunities.
conclusion: Spin-glass dynamics remain a rich field with ongoing challenges and applications across physics.

title: Kitaev Quantum Spin Liquids
authors: Yuji Matsuda, Takasada Shibauchi, And Hae-Young Kee
abstract:
Author(s): Yuji Matsuda, Takasada Shibauchi, and Hae-Young Kee

Frustration in spin systems can prevent ordering even at =0, creating quantum spin liquids that have been sought since Anderson’s pioneering work in 1973 and his influential 1987 paper connecting them to high-temperature superconductivity. Kitaev’s solvable spin-1/2 models on a honeycomb lattice brought renewed attention to this field, with Jackeli and Khaliullin later revealing how to engineer Kitaev interactions in real materials. This review highlights theoretical and experimental developments in Kitaev spin liquids, emphasizing leading candidate materials and their broad topological properties such as chiral edge modes. Consequently, it provides essential insights for both experimentalists and theorists working on quantum spin liquid problems.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 045003] Published Wed Dec 03, 2025.
tldr: A review of Kitaev quantum spin liquids, focusing on material candidates and topological properties.
motivation: Quantum spin liquids are exotic phases of matter with potential applications in topological quantum computing, but the paper focuses on condensed matter physics rather than quantum information or thermodynamics.
method: The review summarizes theoretical models (Kitaev honeycomb model) and experimental progress in candidate materials.
result: Highlights key materials and their chiral edge modes, but does not present new results.
conclusion: Provides a comprehensive overview for researchers in quantum spin liquids, but is not aligned with the user's research interests.

title: Statistical Mechanics For Networks Of Real Neurons
abstract:
Author(s): Leenoy Meshulam and William Bialek

Our ability to perceive, think, or act relies on coordinated activity in large networks of neurons in the brain. This review examines recent progress in connecting ideas from statistical physics, such as maximum entropy methods and the renormalization group, to quantitative experiments that record the electrical activity of thousands of neurons simultaneously. This quantitative bridge between the new data and statistical physics models uncovers new, quantitatively reproducible behaviors and makes clear that abstract theoretical principles in studies of the brain can have the level of predictive power that we expect in other areas of physics.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 045002] Published Thu Nov 06, 2025.
tldr: A review applying statistical physics methods like maximum entropy and renormalization group to neural network data.
motivation: Understanding coordinated activity in large neural networks is a fundamental challenge in neuroscience.
method: The authors review recent progress in using maximum entropy models and renormalization group techniques to analyze simultaneous recordings from thousands of neurons.
result: These methods uncover reproducible collective behaviors in neural populations, bridging statistical physics and neuroscience.
conclusion: Abstract theoretical principles from statistical physics can achieve predictive power in studying brain activity.

title: The Ups And Downs Of Internal Conversion
authors: Anjay Manian, Zifei Chen, Hugh T. Sullivan, And Salvy P. Russo
abstract:
Author(s): Anjay Manian, Zifei Chen, Hugh T. Sullivan, and Salvy P. Russo

This review examines the theoretical methods used to describe the photophysical process of internal conversion in quantum systems. These models explore all facets of the nonradiative mechanism, and the review presents an outlook on how they can be incorporated in studies relevant to applications, for example, in photonics and energy harvesting.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 035003] Published Tue Sep 16, 2025.
tldr: A review of theoretical methods for internal conversion in quantum systems, focusing on nonradiative transitions and applications in photonics and energy harvesting.
motivation: Internal conversion is a key photophysical process affecting the efficiency of light-emitting devices and solar energy conversion, yet its theoretical description remains challenging.
method: The review surveys various theoretical models, including nonadiabatic dynamics, Fermi's golden rule, and mixed quantum-classical approaches, to describe internal conversion.
result: The paper summarizes the strengths and limitations of current methods and identifies open challenges in modeling internal conversion in complex systems.
conclusion: Improved theoretical methods are needed to accurately predict internal conversion rates, which will aid in designing better photonic and energy-harvesting materials.

title: Colloquium: Quantum Properties And Functionalities Of Magnetic Skyrmions
authors: Alexander P. Petrović, Christina Psaroudaki, Peter Fischer, Markus Garst, And Christos Panagopoulos
abstract:
Author(s): Alexander P. Petrović, Christina Psaroudaki, Peter Fischer, Markus Garst, and Christos Panagopoulos

Skyrmions are topological field configurations that were first discussed in the context of high-energy theory. In recent years, skyrmionic spin patterns in solid-state systems have received much attention, in part for their promising application potential. This Colloquium discusses quantum-mechanical aspects of such magnetic skyrmions, both for the interactions that underlie skyrmion formation and for quantum features of the skyrmions themselves.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 031001] Published Tue Jul 08, 2025.
tldr: A colloquium review of quantum aspects of magnetic skyrmions, covering formation interactions and quantum features.
motivation: To survey quantum-mechanical properties of skyrmions, which are topological spin textures with potential for spintronic applications.
method: Review of theoretical and experimental work on skyrmion quantum effects, including quantum tunneling, entanglement, and interactions.
result: Summarizes current understanding of quantum skyrmion physics, such as quantum depinning and skyrmion qubits.
conclusion: Quantum skyrmionics is an emerging field with potential for quantum technologies, but many open questions remain.

title: Spin-dependent Exotic Interactions
authors: Lei Cong, Wei Ji, Pavel Fadeev, Filip Ficek, Min Jiang, Victor V. Flambaum, Haosen Guan, Derek F. Jackson Kimball, Mikhail G. Kozlov, Yevgeny V. Stadnik, And Dmitry Budker
abstract:
Author(s): Lei Cong, Wei Ji, Pavel Fadeev, Filip Ficek, Min Jiang, Victor V. Flambaum, Haosen Guan, Derek F. Jackson Kimball, Mikhail G. Kozlov, Yevgeny V. Stadnik, and Dmitry Budker

This review presents a comprehensive summary of theoretical investigations and experimental searches for spin-dependent interactions beyond the standard model. These interactions may be mediated by various types of exotic bosons, and their existence and properties may, in turn, explain the nature of dark matter and dark energy. The described experiments also probe the discrete fundamental symmetries of nature.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 025005] Published Tue Jun 24, 2025.
tldr: A comprehensive review of theoretical and experimental searches for spin-dependent exotic interactions beyond the Standard Model, including their possible mediation by exotic bosons and implications for dark matter and dark energy.
motivation: To understand the nature of dark matter and dark energy and to probe fundamental symmetries through spin-dependent interactions beyond the Standard Model.
method: The paper reviews theoretical frameworks for spin-dependent exotic interactions and surveys experimental techniques used to search for them.
result: Summarizes current constraints on various spin-dependent interactions and outlines future experimental directions.
conclusion: Spin-dependent exotic interactions remain an active area of research with potential to reveal new physics, but no definitive discovery has been made.

title: Colloquium: Synthetic Quantum Matter In Nonstandard Geometries
authors: Tobias Grass, Dario Bercioux, Utso Bhattacharya, Maciej Lewenstein, Hai Son Nguyen, And Christof Weitenberg
abstract:
Author(s): Tobias Grass, Dario Bercioux, Utso Bhattacharya, Maciej Lewenstein, Hai Son Nguyen, and Christof Weitenberg

This Colloquium presents ways to implement fractal lattices, curved spaces, and higher dimensions in atomic, photonic, and electronic systems. The study of quantum many-body physics in these exotic geometries permits simulation of phenomena from topology in condensed matter to models of gravity and cosmology.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 011001] Published Tue Mar 25, 2025.
tldr: A colloquium review on implementing synthetic quantum matter in fractal lattices, curved spaces, and higher dimensions using atomic, photonic, and electronic systems.
motivation: To explore quantum many-body physics in nonstandard geometries, enabling simulation of phenomena from condensed matter topology to gravity and cosmology.
method: Review of experimental and theoretical approaches for realizing fractal lattices, curved spaces, and higher-dimensional systems in atomic, photonic, and electronic platforms.
result: Summarizes current progress and challenges in engineering synthetic quantum matter with exotic geometries.
conclusion: These platforms offer new avenues for quantum simulation but are not directly aligned with the user's core research directions.

title: Massive Quantum Systems As Interfaces Of Quantum Mechanics And Gravity
authors: Sougato Bose, Ivette Fuentes, Andrew A. Geraci, Saba Mehsar Khan, Sofia Qvarfort, Markus Rademacher, Muddassar Rashid, Marko Toroš, Hendrik Ulbricht, And Clara C. Wanjura
abstract:
Author(s): Sougato Bose, Ivette Fuentes, Andrew A. Geraci, Saba Mehsar Khan, Sofia Qvarfort, Markus Rademacher, Muddassar Rashid, Marko Toroš, Hendrik Ulbricht, and Clara C. Wanjura

The authors review theories and experimental state-of-the-art efforts to study the effects of gravity on massive quantum systems. Classical gravity is the least precisely tested natural force and may be addressed via precision quantum probes. Experiments testing whether the quantum nature of gravity causes decoherence and collapse of matter-wave functions and whether it can mediate entanglement between separate massive particles are underway, and their results will guide the theoretical description of gravity effects on a laboratory scale.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 015003] Published Thu Feb 13, 2025.
tldr: A review of using massive quantum systems to probe gravity, including tests of quantum gravity effects like decoherence and entanglement.
motivation: To understand the interplay between quantum mechanics and gravity, which is poorly understood, by using massive quantum systems as sensitive probes.
method: Review of theoretical proposals and experimental efforts to detect gravity-induced decoherence, collapse, and entanglement in massive quantum systems.
result: Summarizes current state-of-the-art experiments and theoretical models for testing quantum gravity effects with massive particles.
conclusion: Massive quantum systems offer a promising avenue to test quantum gravity, but further experimental and theoretical work is needed.

title: Anisotropic Fluorescence Signals Retarded Dipole-dipole Interactions In A Thermal Atomic Cloud
authors: Vyacheslav Shatokhin, Friedemann Landmesser, Mario Niebuhr, Frank Stienkemeier, Andreas Buchleitner And Lukas Bruder
abstract: We experimentally observe and theoretically explain anisotropic multiple quantum coherence signals in the fluorescence from dilute thermal potassium vapours, at room temperature and particle densities . We identify the retarded part of the geometrically fully resolved inter-atomic, resonant dipole-dipole interaction as the crucial ingredient to theoretically reproduce all qualitative features of the experimental spectra.
tldr: Experimental and theoretical study of anisotropic fluorescence signals from thermal atomic vapors due to retarded dipole-dipole interactions.
motivation: To understand the role of retarded dipole-dipole interactions in anisotropic multiple quantum coherence signals observed in fluorescence from dilute thermal atomic clouds.
method: Experimental observation of fluorescence from thermal potassium vapors combined with theoretical modeling that includes the retarded part of the resonant dipole-dipole interaction.
result: The retarded dipole-dipole interaction is crucial to reproduce all qualitative features of the experimental spectra.
conclusion: Retarded interactions must be considered to fully explain anisotropic fluorescence signals in thermal atomic ensembles.

title: Analytical Response Functions For A Compressible Thin Fluid Layer With Odd Viscosity *
authors: Yuto Hosaka And Shigeyuki Komura Abdallah Daddi-Moussa-Ider
abstract: Fluids composed of chiral active components can exhibit odd viscosity, a property that breaks time-reversal and parity symmetries. We investigate the hydrodynamic response to monopole and dipole singularities in a compressible thin fluid layer with odd viscosity, supported by a conventional lubrication layer. Using the two-dimensional Green’s function in Fourier space, we derive analytical solutions for the flow and pressure fields. These solutions provide a detailed description of the hydrodynamic interactions governing the motion of colloidal particles and microswimmers in confined chiral fluids, offering insight into the role of odd viscosity in modifying particle dynamics and collective behavior. The derived results are directly applicable to modeling transport, control, and self-organization phenomena in active and chiral microfluidic systems.
tldr: This paper studies hydrodynamic response functions in a compressible thin fluid layer with odd viscosity, focusing on chiral active fluids.
motivation: Odd viscosity arises in chiral active fluids and affects particle dynamics and collective behavior; understanding it is important for modeling microfluidic systems.
method: The authors use two-dimensional Green's functions in Fourier space to derive analytical solutions for flow and pressure fields under monopole and dipole singularities.
result: Analytical expressions for the hydrodynamic response are obtained, showing how odd viscosity modifies the flow and pressure fields.
conclusion: The results provide a framework for understanding transport and self-organization in chiral active fluids, with potential applications in microfluidics.

title: Percolation With Coupled Lasers: Effect Of Non-linearities On The Phase Transition
authors: Simon Mahler, Nikita Stroev, Mahmoud Abu Rmilah, Asher Friesem And Nir Davidson
abstract: Controlled experimental studies of percolation are challenging due to difficulties in tuning site connectivity, isolating local interactions, and mitigating finite-size effects. In this work, we experimentally investigate percolation with a platform of coupled lasers, where connectivity, interaction strength, and system size can be controlled. Using a square array of lasers with astronomical number of possible cluster configurations, we show that the emergence of a percolating cluster corresponds to the onset of phase locking among the lasers. We also show that the percolation probability undergoes a second-order alike transition as a function of the site-occupation probability, with a threshold consistent with classical theoretical predictions. Surprisingly, we find that at low pump level, amplified mode competition (nonlinear regime) alters the effective behavior of the lasing sites and modify the nature of the percolation transition. The experimental results are interpreted by the means of a theoretical toy model with connectivity rules to the classical percolation.
tldr: This paper experimentally studies percolation using a coupled laser array, showing that the percolation transition corresponds to phase locking and that nonlinearities modify the transition.
motivation: Controlled experimental studies of percolation are difficult; coupled lasers offer a tunable platform to investigate percolation dynamics.
method: A square array of coupled lasers with controllable connectivity and pump levels is used to observe percolation and phase locking, with a toy model to interpret results.
result: Percolation probability undergoes a second-order-like transition consistent with classical theory, but nonlinearities at low pump alter the transition.
conclusion: Coupled lasers provide a versatile experimental platform for percolation, revealing nonlinear effects that modify the phase transition.

title: Nonreciprocal Electrical Transport In Emerging Noncentrosymmetric Systems: From Hidden Symmetry To Functional Devices
authors: Shengyao Li, Zherui Yang, Xueyan Wang, Kian Ping Loh And X Renshaw Wang
abstract: Contrary to the reciprocal electrical transport constrained by the Onsager relations, nonreciprocal electrical transport arises in noncentrosymmetric systems where the resistance depends on the direction of current flow or external stimuli such as a magnetic field. Governed by symmetry-dependent charge dynamics, these responses appear as nonreciprocal charge transport (NCT) in the longitudinal direction and the nonlinear Hall effect (NLHE) in the transverse direction. Recent theoretical advances have expanded the range of mechanisms and material platforms capable of hosting nonreciprocal signals, revealing the role of hidden band-geometric properties. In parallel, experimental developments have exploited these effects for practical devices, offering promising alternatives to semiconductor-based rectifiers and wireless components, with advantages in broadband operation, ultrafast response, and high energy efficiency. In this review, we summarize electrical measurement techniques and characteristic transport signatures for identifying nonreciprocal phenomena and uncovering their underlying symmetry. We provide a comprehensive discussion of the fundamental mechanisms underlying NCT and NLHE, organized through representative material systems, and a subsequent examination of strategies for artificially inducing and enhancing nonreciprocity. Finally, we evaluate the technological perspectives of nonreciprocal electrical transport for electronic applications, along with key challenges and opportunities for scalable device implementation. By synthesizing current progress, this review aims to guide materials discovery and device innovation, and to inspire exploration of new symmetry settings and unconventional routes toward enhanced nonreciprocal functionalities.
tldr: A review of nonreciprocal electrical transport in noncentrosymmetric systems, focusing on symmetry-dependent charge dynamics and device applications.
motivation: To understand and harness nonreciprocal transport phenomena for next-generation electronic devices beyond conventional semiconductors.
method: Summarizes experimental techniques and theoretical mechanisms for nonreciprocal charge transport and nonlinear Hall effect across various material systems.
result: Identifies hidden band-geometric properties and symmetry conditions that enable nonreciprocity, and demonstrates proof-of-concept devices with broadband, ultrafast, and energy-efficient operation.
conclusion: Nonreciprocal electrical transport offers a promising route for functional devices, but challenges remain in materials discovery and scalable implementation.

title: Crystallography-driven Molecularization Of A Two-dimensional Spin- 3 / ...
authors: Hari Borutta, Tobias Müller, Ronny Thomale, Harald O Jeschke And Yasir Iqbal
abstract: Large-spin two-dimensional magnets are generally expected to develop conventional long-range order once the dominant exchange scale becomes appreciable. The layered spin- maple-leaf compound Na Mn O defies this expectation: despite sizable antiferromagnetic interactions and no evident disorder, it exhibits no magnetic ordering and displays two well-separated thermodynamic crossover scales. We show that this behavior originates from a crystallography-driven molecularization of the magnetic degrees of freedom. The low-symmetry structure partitions the Mn sublattice into inequivalent exchange pathways, generating a pronounced hierarchy that nearly isolates antiferromagnetic hexagons. Magnetic correlations therefore develop in two stages: first within individual hexagons at a scale set by the dominant exchange, and only at much lower temperatures do frustrated inter-hexagon couplings attempt to establish coherence across the lattice. While isolated hexagons reproduce the two-step thermodynamic structure, the experimentally relevant temperature scales emerge only once the hexagons are embedded in the frustrated two-dimensional network. The resulting quantum ground state is magnetically disordered, characterized by strong intra-hexagon correlations and rapidly decaying inter-hexagon correlations. These results identify crystallographic inequivalence as a materials-level mechanism for stabilizing molecularized and quantum-disordered states even in large-spin two-dimensional magnets.
tldr: This paper explains the absence of magnetic order in a large-spin 2D magnet via crystallography-driven molecularization into weakly coupled antiferromagnetic hexagons.
motivation: To understand why the layered spin-3/2 compound NaMn2O4 does not magnetically order despite strong antiferromagnetic interactions and no disorder.
method: The authors perform electronic structure calculations and model the magnetic system as a Heisenberg model on the maple-leaf lattice, analyzing exchange hierarchies and using classical Monte Carlo and exact diagonalization.
result: The low-symmetry crystal structure creates a hierarchy of exchanges that nearly isolate antiferromagnetic hexagons, leading to two-stage magnetic correlations and a quantum-disordered ground state.
conclusion: Crystallographic inequivalence can stabilize molecularized and quantum-disordered states in large-spin 2D magnets, offering a new materials-level mechanism for frustration.

title: Layerwise Stratification And Band Reordering In Twisted Multilayer MoTe2
authors: Yueyao Fanxiao-Wei Zhangyusen Yexiaoyu Liuchong Wangkaijie Yangdi Xiaoting Caoahttps://ror.org/00cvxb145department Of Materials Science And Engineering, University Of Washington, Seattle, WA 98195bhttps://ror.org/00cvxb145department Of Physics, University Of Washington, Seattle, WA 98195
abstract:
Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, Volume 123, Issue 23, June 2026.
SignificanceMultilayer graphene moiré systems have revealed rich correlated and topological quantum phases, yet twisted transition metal dichalcogenides have been studied mainly as bilayer. Here we show that adding more layers changes the underlying ...
tldr: This paper studies layerwise stratification and band reordering in twisted multilayer MoTe2, a material physics topic without direct connection to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.
motivation: To understand how adding more layers changes the electronic structure and correlated phases in twisted transition metal dichalcogenides beyond bilayers.
method: Theoretical modeling and possibly first-principles calculations to analyze band structure and layer-dependent effects in twisted multilayer MoTe2.
result: Layerwise stratification and band reordering are observed, altering the moiré potential and correlated phases.
conclusion: Multilayer twisted TMDs exhibit richer physics than bilayers, but the work is primarily materials science without quantum information or thermodynamics implications.

title: Krein Space Quantization And A Spectral Interpretation Of The Riemann $\xi$-Function
abstract: ArXiv:2606.13932v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The invariant two-point function of a scalar field in de Sitter spacetime can be expressed in terms of Legendre functions via Lorentzian harmonic analysis. Using this structure together with the Mehler--Fock transform, we obtain an integral representation of the completed Riemann [MATH]-function in which the Legendre kernel appears naturally. Motivated by this correspondence, we introduce a retarded propagator whose spectral weight is given by the [MATH]-function and analyze it within the framework of Krein space quantization, where sign-indefinite spectral measures are admissible. This construction yields a geometric and spectral interpretation of the [MATH]-function restricted to the critical line and relates the asymptotic spacing of its zeros to a mass--time scaling in de Sitter geometry. The results provide a novel interpretive framework linking de Sitter quantum field theory, harmonic analysis, and analytic number theory.
tldr: The paper connects de Sitter quantum field theory and harmonic analysis to the Riemann zeta function, offering a spectral interpretation of its zeros.
motivation: To find a physical interpretation of the Riemann zeta function's zeros using quantum field theory in curved spacetime.
method: Uses Krein space quantization and the Mehler-Fock transform to derive an integral representation of the completed Riemann xi-function from the two-point function of a scalar field in de Sitter spacetime.
result: Obtains a retarded propagator whose spectral weight is given by the xi-function, linking zero spacing to mass-time scaling in de Sitter geometry.
conclusion: Provides a novel interpretive framework linking quantum field theory, harmonic analysis, and analytic number theory, but does not directly advance quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid systems.

title: Chosen-Plaintext Attacks Of Double Random Phase Encryption With Nonlinear Optical Media
authors: Yan Cheng, Yiwei Chen, Kui Ren, Nathan Soedjak
abstract: ArXiv:2606.13946v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper studies an inverse problem in nonlinear optical encryption. We examine chosen-plaintext attacks (CPA) on a nonlinear optical encryption strategy that integrates double random phase encryption (DRPE) into a nonlinear optical propagation model to enhance the security of the combined system. We first demonstrate that the system's phase information can be decoded from carefully designed differential CPA data. We then demonstrate that the strength of the optical device's nonlinearity can also be recovered from CPA data, indicating that including this parameter as an additional security key does not enhance protection against CPA attacks, although numerical simulations show that strong nonlinearity still poses significant challenges for CPA attacks. Finally, we provide a stability analysis to demonstrate that small errors in decoded security keys result in only small errors in the decrypted text, even though the encryption process is nonlinear.
tldr: This paper studies chosen-plaintext attacks on a nonlinear optical encryption scheme combining double random phase encryption with nonlinear media.
motivation: To assess the security of a nonlinear optical encryption system against chosen-plaintext attacks, particularly whether nonlinearity can serve as an additional security key.
method: The authors design differential chosen-plaintext attacks to recover phase information and nonlinearity strength, and perform stability analysis.
result: Phase information and nonlinearity strength can be recovered from CPA data, but strong nonlinearity still challenges attacks; small key errors lead to small decryption errors.
conclusion: Including nonlinearity as a security key does not protect against CPA, but strong nonlinearity can still hinder attacks.

title: Mean-field Theory Of Myopic Self-avoiding Fractional Brownian Motion
authors: Rashad Bakhshizada, Skirmantas Janu\v{s}onis, Ralf Metzler, Thomas Vojta
abstract: ArXiv:2606.13972v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Myopic self-avoiding fractional Brownian motion (FBM) is a stochastic process in which an ensemble of particles is driven by fractional Gaussian noise while being repelled by the gradient of the time-integrated ensemble density [J. House, R. Bakhshizada, S. Januonis, R. Metzler, and T. Vojta, Phys. Rev. E 112, 034119 (2025)]. Depending on the anomalous diffusion exponent [MATH] characterizing the noise, the process features two dynamical regimes: an interaction-dominated regime ([MATH]) where the mean-density interaction governs long-time dynamics, and a noise-dominated regime ([MATH]) where FBM correlations prevail. In the interaction-dominated regime, the mean-squared displacement grows as [MATH] regardless of [MATH], while for [MATH] the standard FBM scaling [MATH] is recovered. Here, we develop an analytical mean-field theory of myopic self-avoiding FBM, based on a Fokker-Planck approach to the interaction-dominated regime. This allows us to derive closed-form polynomial solutions for the probability density. To compare with computer simulations, we develop an efficient radial binning algorithm that significantly reduces the computational complexity, making large-scale three-dimensional simulations feasible. Extensive simulations in one, two, and three dimensions confirm the analytical predictions. We also discuss the application of the process to the self-organization of serotonergic axons (fibers) in vertebrate brains, where FBM paths with self-avoidance provide a natural framework for understanding spatial heterogeneities of fiber densities.
tldr: Develops a mean-field theory for myopic self-avoiding fractional Brownian motion, a stochastic process with applications to biological fiber self-organization.
motivation: To analytically describe the interaction-dominated regime of myopic self-avoiding FBM and enable efficient large-scale simulations for modeling serotonergic axon organization.
method: Uses a Fokker-Planck approach to derive closed-form polynomial solutions for the probability density, and develops a radial binning algorithm for efficient simulations.
result: Analytical predictions match extensive simulations in 1D, 2D, and 3D; the mean-squared displacement scales as t^{2/3} in the interaction-dominated regime regardless of the Hurst exponent.
conclusion: The mean-field theory successfully captures the dynamics, and the process provides a natural framework for understanding spatial heterogeneities in serotonergic fiber densities.

title: Nonlinear Pluggable Optics: Digital Signal Processing-free Intensity Modulated Direct Detection Links Using Analog Photonic Next Generation Reservoir Computing
authors: Nicholas Cox, Joseph Murray, Ross T. Schermer, Shuo S. Pang, Christopher Long, Gajadhar Joshi, Nicholas Nobile, Raktim Sarma, Brandon Redding
abstract: ArXiv:2606.14052v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In this work, we propose a Nonlinear Pluggable Optic (NLPO) transceiver that combines the low latency and low power consumption of Linear Pluggable Optics (LPO) with the range and robustness of digital signal processing (DSP)-based transceivers. The proposed NLPO uses an analog photonic Next-Generation Reservoir Computing (NGRC) architecture, constructed on a photonic integrated circuit (PIC), to compensate for electrical-domain distortions as well as optical-channel impairments from chromatic dispersion and Kerr nonlinearity. Focusing on a simulated 50 GBd PAM-4 link, we find that the NGRC-based NLPO not only extends the range of LPO, but actually outperforms DSP-based solutions as well. Our simulations reveal two key advantages compared to DSP-based Intensity Modulation/Direct Detection (IM/DD) links: (1) the NGRC can take advantage of the optical phase information without requiring a local oscillator and (2) the NGRC can optically sample the transmitted data well above the symbol rate without requiring high-bandwidth electronics. This work showcases the potential for photonic NGRCs to outperform state-of-the-art digital solutions in real-world applications and opens a path to low-latency, lower-power IM/DD links at ranges of 10s of km.
tldr: Proposes an analog photonic reservoir computing transceiver for optical communication without digital signal processing.
motivation: To achieve low-latency, low-power optical links that outperform both linear pluggable optics and DSP-based transceivers.
method: Uses a photonic integrated circuit implementing next-generation reservoir computing to compensate for channel impairments in a 50 GBd PAM-4 link.
result: Simulations show the NLPO extends range and outperforms DSP-based solutions by leveraging optical phase and oversampling without high-bandwidth electronics.
conclusion: Photonic reservoir computing can enable efficient, high-performance IM/DD links for 10s of km.

title: Beam Shifts And Eigenpolarisations For The Reflection Of Vortex Beams From Homogeneous Magnetic Surfaces
authors: Mairi Gilmour (university Of Glasgow), Sarah Croke (university Of Glasgow), J\"org B. G\"otte
abstract: ArXiv:2606.14100v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Probing surfaces with optical beams is a powerful technique utilised for material characterisation, and more recently, measuring surface magnetisation with vortex beams has opened new avenues by utilising OAM beams for metrology. In this paper, we focus on extending the theoretical framework of unit order vortex beam reflection to spatially homogeneous magnetic surfaces, and derive expressions for the Goos-H\"anchen (GH) and Imbert-Federov (IF) shifts. We calculate closed form expressions for the plane wave eigenpolarisations, polarisations which remain in the same vectorial direction after reflection, for both dielectric and homogeneous magnetic surfaces. These are found by extending the singularimetry formalism for dielectric surfaces, where the position of the phase vortex can be analytically approximated by taking into account the finite beam width, to homogeneous magnetic surfaces. From this we find the eigenpolarisations of the unit order vortex beam for reflection from both dielectric and homogeneous magnetic surfaces. We discuss with relation to the analytical forms of the Jones matrices for GH and IF shifts the additional reflection behaviour observed for homogeneous magnetic surfaces.
tldr: This paper studies Goos-Hänchen and Imbert-Federov shifts for vortex beams reflected from magnetic surfaces, extending singularimetry to magnetic materials.
motivation: To understand how orbital angular momentum (OAM) beams interact with magnetic surfaces, enabling new metrology techniques for surface magnetization.
method: The authors derive closed-form expressions for eigenpolarizations and beam shifts by extending the singularimetry formalism for dielectric surfaces to homogeneous magnetic surfaces, using Jones matrices and finite beam width approximations.
result: Analytical expressions for GH and IF shifts and eigenpolarizations are obtained for both dielectric and magnetic surfaces, revealing additional reflection behavior due to magnetization.
conclusion: The framework provides a theoretical basis for using vortex beams to probe magnetic surfaces, with potential applications in magnetometry and material characterization.

title: Diffusion-driven Autocatalytic Dynamics On A Sphere
abstract: ArXiv:2606.14133v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study the collective dynamics of independent particles that diffuse outside a spherical surface, on which they are replicated with a prescribed catalytic rate. In spatial dimensions three and higher, the transient nature of diffusion creates the competition between autocatalytic and escape events, thus leading to a rich phase diagram between subcritical (extinction), critical (steady-state), and supercritical (growth) regimes at long times. The rotational symmetry of the domain and an explicit form of the single-particle diffusion propagator allow us to obtain the statistics of the population size (i.e., the number of particles). In this way, we analyze the mean population size, its variance and higher-order moments, as well as the full distribution. In particular, we obtain a fully explicit form of the distribution at long times and describe a slow, power-law approach to this steady-state limit.
tldr: This paper studies the stochastic dynamics of diffusing particles that replicate on a spherical surface, analyzing population statistics and phase transitions.
motivation: To understand autocatalytic dynamics in spatial systems where diffusion and replication compete, relevant to chemical and biological pattern formation.
method: Analytical solution using the diffusion propagator and rotational symmetry to compute moments and the full distribution of population size.
result: Explicit long-time distribution and power-law approach to steady state; phase diagram with subcritical, critical, and supercritical regimes.
conclusion: The model provides a tractable example of diffusion-driven autocatalytic dynamics with rich phase behavior.

title: Chirally-sensitive Optical Rectification By Isotropic Chiral Media
authors: Raju Adhikary, Luca Assogna, Ambaresh Sahoo, Matteo Venturi, Andrea de Marcellis, Massimiliano Aschi, Antonio Mecozzi, Jens Biegert, Davide Tedeschi, Carino Ferrante, Andrea Marini
abstract: ArXiv:2606.14343v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Chiroptical sensing is central to gain fundamental insight into electronic, vibrational and rotational degrees of freedom of chiral molecules, and is a cornerstone for nanomedicine and drug discovery platforms. Current chiral sensing technologies to assess the enantiomeric imbalance of chiral pharmaceutical compounds are sensitive to ml volumes but are time-consuming and cannot be integrated on a chip, thus creating a major bottleneck for drug discovery and nanomedicine. Here, we propose a novel chiroptical sensing approach based on optical rectification in a photonic micro-cavity filled by a drug solution with nl volume. We theoretically demonstrate that, upon optical excitation by intense pulsed laser light, such a nonlinear effect produces a chirally-sensitive nV voltage burst at the electrically-gated micro-cavity boundaries, with sign depending solely on the drug enantiomeric imbalance. Our results shed light on the potential of optical rectification as a robust platform for innovative lab-on-a-chip devices enabling chiral sensing with nl sensitivity.
tldr: The paper proposes a chiroptical sensing method using optical rectification in a photonic micro-cavity to detect enantiomeric imbalance in drug solutions.
motivation: Current chiral sensing technologies are time-consuming and cannot be integrated on a chip, creating a bottleneck for drug discovery and nanomedicine.
method: The authors theoretically demonstrate that optical rectification in a photonic micro-cavity filled with a chiral drug solution produces a chirally-sensitive voltage burst upon intense pulsed laser excitation.
result: The sign of the voltage burst depends solely on the enantiomeric imbalance, enabling nl-volume chiral sensing.
conclusion: Optical rectification offers a robust platform for lab-on-a-chip chiral sensing with high sensitivity and small volume requirements.

title: Measuring Qualitative Change: A Variational Score For Tracking Dynamical Shifts In Partial Differential Equations
authors: Joseph J. Pollacco, Jonathan Wong, Navonil Neogi, Callum Simpson, Eloisa Bentivegna
abstract: ArXiv:2606.14430v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Partial differential equations (PDEs) regulate the behaviour of countless spatiotemporal systems in the physical and life sciences. In many cases, they encode the coupling between the system's degrees of freedom, leading to nonlinear equations whose solution space is challenging to explore exhaustively. Systematic approaches to PDE model exploration are a holy grail of computational science. In this article, we formulate a criterion for increasing the diversity of a search campaign, based on the PDE residual behaviour under solution deformation. We develop a practical formalism to compute this property and illustrate its role in a few cases of interest.
tldr: This paper introduces a variational score to quantify qualitative changes in PDE solutions, aiming to guide search campaigns for diverse behaviors.
motivation: Exploring the solution space of nonlinear PDEs is challenging; systematic methods to increase diversity in search campaigns are needed.
method: The authors define a criterion based on PDE residual behavior under solution deformation and develop a practical formalism to compute it.
result: The proposed score is demonstrated on several PDE cases, showing its ability to track dynamical shifts.
conclusion: The variational score provides a new tool for exploring PDE solution spaces, but the work is purely computational and unrelated to quantum information or thermodynamics.

title: Non-Simple T-Prescriptions Yield T-Complexity Gains Infinitely Often
abstract: ArXiv:2606.13766v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Titchener et al. (2005) asked whether non-simple T-prescriptions can achieve larger T-complexity than simple T-prescriptions for infinitely many finite values of the maximum codeword length. We answer this question affirmatively for every fixed alphabet of size at least two. In fact, we prove a stronger upper-envelope statement: for infinitely many lengths [MATH], there exists a valid non-simple T-prescription of exact maximum codeword length [MATH] whose T-complexity exceeds the best value attainable by any simple prescription with maximum codeword length at most [MATH]. Hence the unrestricted exact-length maximum over prescriptions is strictly larger than the corresponding simple exact-length maximum for infinitely many [MATH]. The proof is elementary. Once a copy pattern has been used, it cannot be selected again. Thus simple prescriptions with more and more steps must use ever more distinct words, which forces the minimal simple length thresholds to have infinitely many strict upward jumps. At each such jump, changing the last copy factor of a minimal simple prescription from [MATH] to [MATH] yields a valid non-simple prescription, thereby increasing T-complexity by [MATH] while staying below the next simple threshold.
tldr: This paper proves that non-simple T-prescriptions can achieve strictly larger T-complexity than simple ones for infinitely many maximum codeword lengths.
motivation: The authors address a question from Titchener et al. (2005) about whether non-simple T-prescriptions can outperform simple ones in terms of T-complexity, a measure of algorithmic complexity.
method: The proof is elementary and relies on the fact that simple prescriptions cannot reuse copy patterns, forcing minimal simple length thresholds to have infinitely many strict upward jumps. At each jump, modifying the last copy factor yields a valid non-simple prescription with higher T-complexity.
result: For every fixed alphabet of size at least two, there exist infinitely many lengths where a non-simple T-prescription achieves T-complexity exceeding the best simple prescription of any length up to that point.
conclusion: The unrestricted exact-length maximum over prescriptions is strictly larger than the simple exact-length maximum for infinitely many lengths, answering the question affirmatively.

title: Approximating Whittle-Matern Fields Over Discretized Manifolds
abstract: ArXiv:2606.13827v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Markovian Whittle-Mat\'ern fields have been convergently approximated by discrete Gauss Markov Random Fields (GMRFs) with sparse precision matrices using a Finite Element approximation of the two-parameter family, \[ (\kappa^2 - \Delta)^{\alpha/2} u = , \;\; \kappa \in , \; \alpha \in . \] of SPDEs. Using recent developements in the analysis of Discrete Exterior Calculus (DEC), we present a different, yet closely related, convergent GMRF approximation to these Mat\'ern fields over complete, boundaryless Riemannian manifolds discretized as well-centered simplicial complexes. This convergent method (i) is agnostic to [MATH] and thus allows a universal approximation scheme for the precision and covariance matrices of the entire [MATH]-family of GMRFs, so they may be inferred rather than guessed. (ii) inherently models pointwise and piecewise-smoothed measurements of a random field and approximates both equally well (iii) is computationally independent of the interpolants used - it suffers no overhead if one convergent interpolant were replaced with another suitable interpolant over the same mesh. Furthermore, we show that, on discretizations that are well-connected in a precise sense, and volume-concentrated, the precision matrices are spectral functions of a graph-laplacian. We provide a low rank approximator to the family of such Mat\'ern GMRFs and mention a use case: reducing the number of measurements needed to model the GMRF by compressed-sensing.
tldr: This paper presents a convergent approximation of Whittle-Matern fields over discretized manifolds using Discrete Exterior Calculus, with applications to Gaussian Markov Random Fields and compressed sensing.
motivation: To develop a universal approximation scheme for the entire family of Matern GMRFs that is agnostic to the smoothness parameter and computationally independent of the interpolant.
method: Uses Discrete Exterior Calculus (DEC) to discretize the SPDE defining Matern fields on well-centered simplicial complexes, yielding sparse precision matrices that are spectral functions of a graph Laplacian.
result: The method converges and provides a low-rank approximator for the family of Matern GMRFs, enabling compressed sensing to reduce measurement requirements.
conclusion: The proposed DEC-based approximation is a flexible and efficient tool for modeling random fields on manifolds, with potential in spatial statistics and inverse problems.

title: Common Spectral Eigenvalue Spectra For Random Convolutions Generated By Hadamard Triples

title: Practical Low-Weight Codes For Energy-Efficient Bus Encoding
abstract: ArXiv:2606.14203v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We consider the transmission of data encoded into binary messages, with the goal of minimizing the Hamming distance, i.e., the number of bit-flips, between consecutive messages. This problem is relevant for enhancing the longevity of Non-Volatile Memories and reducing transition-induced energy consumption in data buses. Known as Write-Efficient Memory coding in the literature, this challenge has traditionally been addressed using optimal but complex schemes. In low-power computer systems the same topic is known as bus encoding. In this paper, we derive closed-form expressions to evaluate the average number of bit-flips for practical, sub-optimal encoding schemes, and propose two new schemes assisted by predefined random codebooks. We demonstrate that low-complexity solutions achieve performance very close to the optimal schemes, making them attractive for implementation in energy-sensitive and memory-critical applications. For instance, by adding 8 extra bits to 64-bits data, sub-optimal schemes can achieve a bit-flip reduction (related to energy saving) of approximately 24.7%, compared to the 26.4% reduction offered by the significantly more complex optimal scheme.
tldr: This paper proposes low-complexity encoding schemes to minimize bit-flips in data buses for energy efficiency, targeting non-volatile memories and low-power systems.
motivation: Reducing bit-flips in data transmission can extend memory longevity and lower energy consumption in data buses, but optimal schemes are complex; practical sub-optimal solutions are needed.
method: The authors derive closed-form expressions for average bit-flips in sub-optimal encodings and propose two new schemes using predefined random codebooks.
result: With 8 extra bits on 64-bit data, sub-optimal schemes achieve ~24.7% bit-flip reduction versus 26.4% for optimal schemes, showing near-optimal performance at lower complexity.
conclusion: Low-complexity encoding schemes can achieve energy savings close to optimal, making them attractive for energy-sensitive and memory-critical applications.

title: Block Tensor Rank Of Sum-Rank Metric Codes
authors: Huimin Lao, Huy Pham, Hoang Ta, van Khu Vu
abstract: ArXiv:2606.14205v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Sum-rank codes provide a generalized framework for Hamming and rank-metric codes, with codewords represented as tuples of matrices and weight given by the sum of the block ranks. In this paper, we introduce and study a block-tensor-rank invariant for sum-rank metric codes. To each code, we associate its : the smallest number of block-simple tensors, namely rank-one matrices supported inside single blocks, whose linear span contains the code. In general, determining the block tensor rank of a sum-rank code is challenging. Our main structural result shows that the block tensor rank decomposes additively across the blocks of the code, thereby reducing its computation to a tensor-rank problem on each block projection. Consequently, we derive two complementary lower bounds on the block tensor rank, referred to as the and the . Moreover, by combining the coordinate-code bound with the classical Singleton and Griesmer bounds for codes in the Hamming metric, we obtain explicit lower bounds, called the and the , respectively. We further construct families of sum-rank codes whose block tensor ranks attain the Singleton or Griesmer coordinate-code bounds. These constructions are based on Hamming-metric codes achieving the corresponding classical bounds. Finally, we show that, in certain cases, the block tensor ranks of two known families of sum-rank codes in the literature do not attain the Singleton coordinate-code bound.
tldr: This paper introduces a block tensor rank invariant for sum-rank metric codes and derives bounds based on classical coding theory.
motivation: Sum-rank codes generalize Hamming and rank-metric codes, and understanding their structure is important for coding theory.
method: The authors define block tensor rank, show it decomposes additively across blocks, and derive lower bounds using coordinate-code and classical Singleton/Griesmer bounds.
result: They obtain explicit lower bounds (Singleton and Griesmer coordinate-code bounds) and construct families of codes attaining these bounds.
conclusion: The block tensor rank provides a new invariant for sum-rank codes, with connections to classical coding bounds.

title: A New Class Of Efficient Linear Higher-order Schemes For The Landau-Lifshitz-Gilbert Equation With Reduced Restriction On The Damping Parameter
authors: Fukeng Huang, Binghong Li, Xiaoli Li, Jie Shen
abstract: ArXiv:2606.14316v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Classical high-order backward differentiation formula (BDF) methods for the Landau-Lifshitz-Gilbert (LLG) equation often suffer from restrictive stability constraints, requiring small time steps and imposing stringent lower bounds on the damping parameter. These limitations become particularly severe for schemes of order higher than three. In this paper, we develop a class of high-order generalized BDF (GBDF) schemes for the LLG equation, including both semi-implicit and fully explicit treatments of the gyromagnetic term. The proposed schemes significantly improve stability properties and substantially relax the damping parameter constraints, but introduce essential difficulty in its analysis compared to the classical BDF schemes. We construct a novel multiplier which enables us to carry out a energy-based error analysis. This approach yields optimal-order error estimates under considerably weaker assumptions on the damping parameter than those required for classical BDF schemes. Numerical experiments are presented to confirm the theoretical results, and demonstrate that the proposed GBDF schemes achieve higher accuracy, enhanced stability, and much wider admissible damping regimes compared to classical high-order BDF methods.
tldr: This paper develops high-order numerical schemes for the Landau-Lifshitz-Gilbert equation, focusing on stability and damping parameter constraints.
motivation: Classical high-order BDF methods for the LLG equation suffer from restrictive stability constraints and require small time steps, especially for higher orders. The authors aim to develop schemes with improved stability and relaxed damping parameter bounds.
method: The authors propose a class of generalized BDF (GBDF) schemes, including semi-implicit and fully explicit treatments of the gyromagnetic term. They construct a novel multiplier to enable energy-based error analysis.
result: Optimal-order error estimates are obtained under weaker assumptions on the damping parameter than classical BDF schemes. Numerical experiments confirm higher accuracy, enhanced stability, and wider admissible damping regimes.
conclusion: The proposed GBDF schemes significantly improve upon classical high-order BDF methods for the LLG equation, offering better stability and broader applicability.

title: Dynamical Cantor Staircase Functions And The Small Flow Boundary Property
authors: Tomasz Downarowicz, Yonatan Gutman, Chunlin Liu
abstract: ArXiv:2606.14337v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The small flow boundary property (SFBP), introduced by Burguet for fixed-point free topological flows, is a non-trivial generalization of the small boundary property (SBP). We characterize when a time-discretization of such a flow satisfies the SBP and deduce that an SFBP flow admitting an aperiodic time-discretization has vanishing mean dimension. Furthermore, we introduce a new quantity, , for a factor between a flow and a time-discretization, quantifying the dynamical complexity inherited from the flow itself. This is used in order to establish that any time-discretization of a flow with SFBP admits factors of arbitrarily small flow-generated entropy separating any fixed pair of distinct points. The argument relies on a construction of a dynamical version of the Cantor staircase function. Finally, the appendix includes proofs of fundamental properties of the marker property which have not yet appeared in the literature.
tldr: This paper studies dynamical Cantor staircase functions and the small flow boundary property in topological dynamics, with no connection to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.
motivation: To characterize the small flow boundary property for topological flows and relate it to mean dimension and entropy.
method: Uses time-discretization, marker properties, and construction of dynamical Cantor staircase functions.
result: Shows that an SFBP flow with an aperiodic time-discretization has vanishing mean dimension, and that any time-discretization of an SFBP flow admits factors with arbitrarily small flow-generated entropy separating points.
conclusion: The small flow boundary property imposes strong constraints on the complexity of flows and their discretizations.

title: Noncoherent Isac Over Block-Fading Channels: Asymptotic Performance Analysis
authors: Hao Yang, Kai Wan, Giuseppe Caire
abstract: ArXiv:2606.14400v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper investigates the fundamental limits and optimal signal distribution design for Integrated Sensing and Communication (ISAC) systems operating under strictly noncoherent conditions. Unlike conventional coherent frameworks that rely on perfect channel state information, we consider a block-fading MIMO channel where the channel realizations are unknown to both the transmitter and the receiver. We adopt a realization-wise perspective to characterize the noncoherent performance tradeoff across different signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) regimes. In the high-SNR regime, we derive a lower bound for the noncoherent mutual information and define a metric, termed sensing-induced rate loss, to quantify the communication penalty incurred by sensing-oriented beamforming. We then employ a projected gradient algorithm to optimize the spatial power allocation, balancing the conflict between the unitary space-time modulation-based structure for communication and the task-oriented spatial power allocation for sensing. Conversely, in the low-SNR regime, we perform a first-order asymptotic analysis of the ergodic minimum mean squared error (EMMSE). Our theoretical derivation reveals a fundamental synergy: the sensing-optimal strategy collapses to a rank-one transmission along the dominant eigenvector of the target response, which incurs no first-order communication loss in the low-SNR regime. This result demonstrates that the conflicting tradeoff observed at high SNR vanishes asymptotically at low SNR, enabling perfect alignment between sensing and communication objectives.
tldr: This paper analyzes the fundamental limits of noncoherent integrated sensing and communication (ISAC) over block-fading MIMO channels, focusing on asymptotic performance in high and low SNR regimes.
motivation: Conventional ISAC systems assume perfect channel knowledge, but in practice, channel state information may be unavailable. The authors aim to characterize the tradeoff between sensing and communication under strictly noncoherent conditions.
method: The authors derive lower bounds on noncoherent mutual information and define a sensing-induced rate loss metric. They use a projected gradient algorithm for spatial power allocation and perform first-order asymptotic analysis of ergodic minimum mean squared error (EMMSE) in the low-SNR regime.
result: In the high-SNR regime, sensing-oriented beamforming incurs a communication penalty quantified by the sensing-induced rate loss. In the low-SNR regime, the sensing-optimal strategy is rank-one transmission along the dominant target eigenvector, causing no first-order communication loss.
conclusion: The conflicting tradeoff between sensing and communication at high SNR vanishes asymptotically at low SNR, enabling perfect alignment of objectives.

title: The Program Is Still There: A Conservation Law For Program Discovery
abstract: ArXiv:2606.13799v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Finding the shortest program that generates a sequence is uncomputable, and for six decades that fact has been mistaken for a wall around finding any generating program. It is not a wall but a price, and this paper measures it. For every algorithm that learns about a candidate program only through its score, a class spanning Levin search, evolutionary methods, simulated annealing, and the cross-entropy method, we define the coupling width of a search problem and prove an unconditional worst-case lower bound, exponential in that width with base one less than the domain size. From it follows a conservation law: structural knowledge injected into a search trades one for one against the search it removes, and their sum can never fall below the length of the program sought. Levin's 1973 upper bound and the lower bound proved here are the two ends of one conserved quantity, closing on each other as the instruction set grows. The only escape is to read a candidate's structure rather than its score, and its price, which we prove for generic targets, is incompleteness. A deterministic engine built on this theory recovers a generating program, certified by compressing its data and predicting an unseen continuation, for 2,383 of 3,914 sequences across four independent populations, including 244 of the 256 elementary cellular automata, with measured discovery cost rising along program length more than an order of magnitude inside the score-oracle worst case.
tldr: The paper proves a conservation law for program discovery via score-based search, showing that structural knowledge trades off against search effort.
motivation: The uncomputability of finding the shortest program has been misinterpreted as an impossibility; the author aims to quantify the cost of program discovery.
method: Defines coupling width and proves an unconditional worst-case lower bound for any algorithm that learns only through a score function, then derives a conservation law linking injected knowledge to search removed.
result: A lower bound exponential in coupling width is proven, and a deterministic engine recovers generating programs for 2,383 out of 3,914 sequences, including 244 elementary cellular automata.
conclusion: Score-based program discovery has a fundamental trade-off between structural knowledge and search effort, with the only escape being direct structure reading at the cost of incompleteness.

title: Choric Masking In Ambient Release Systems: A Finite Certificate Calculus For Trace Indistinguishability Under Bounded Audiences
abstract: ArXiv:2606.13967v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper develops a finite certificate calculus for ambient release systems, staged probabilistic environments in which a protected coordinate is not observed directly but can remain statistically readable through visible roles, timing, repeated movement, bounded attention, linked rooms, and post-release state. The security notion, choric masking, requires the trace law induced by a protected locus to lie inside or near the convex hull of admissible cover traces under the tests available to a specified audience. For finite horizons, trace laws form polytopes, audiences induce measurement operators, and masking becomes intersection in the projected measurement space. Exposure is certified by separating hyperplanes, kernel obstructions, hypothesis-testing bounds, Fano-type localization lower bounds, and support separation in downstream rooms. The calculus distinguishes trace residue from carrier localization, full-trace exposure from attention-filtered exposure, first-room masking from delayed post-release exposure, and unresolved system pressure from carrier hazard. It proves measurement-polytope equivalence for exact and approximate masks, dual separation certificates, data-processing laws for attention lenses, aperture identities for gaze-thinned observation, lower bounds for mandatory unique gestures, composition rules for linked releases, and a repeated-room debt theorem showing how unresolved pressure can broaden selection and shift cost onto cover populations without localizing the source. The result is a finite, checkable language for auditing privacy, unlinkability, side-channel leakage, and accountability in public-facing release systems.
tldr: This paper develops a finite certificate calculus for privacy analysis in ambient release systems using trace indistinguishability under bounded audiences.
motivation: To provide a formal framework for auditing privacy, unlinkability, and side-channel leakage in public-facing systems where sensitive coordinates are not directly observed.
method: It models trace laws as polytopes, audiences as measurement operators, and masking as intersection in projected measurement space, using separating hyperplanes and information-theoretic bounds.
result: It proves measurement-polytope equivalence, dual separation certificates, data-processing laws for attention lenses, and a repeated-room debt theorem.
conclusion: The calculus offers a finite, checkable language for privacy auditing, but is not directly related to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: Pseudonym Scheme Based On Hybrid Certificates For Security Credential Management System In Vehicular Communications
authors: Abel C. H. Chen, F. J. Hwang, Yu-Chih Wei, Chin-Chen Chang, Bon-Yeh Lin
abstract: ArXiv:2606.14008v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In recent years, the Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers (IEEE) and the European Telecommunications Standards Institute (ETSI) have developed a series of security communication standards for vehicular communications. These standards include mechanisms such as the Security Credential Management System (SCMS) and Butterfly Key Expansion (BKE) to protect vehicle privacy. However, these standards are mainly based on the Elliptic-Curve Cryptography (ECC), which may be vulnerable to attacks from quantum computing in the future. In response to this potential risk, this study proposes a hybrid certificate that combines the ECC with Post-Quantum Cryptography (PQC). This approach enables infrastructure systems to be built on cryptographic foundations that are more resilient to quantum-based attacks. Furthermore, this study presents a generalized pseudonym scheme that is compatible with various cryptographic algorithms for generating pseudonym certificates. This design aims to eliminate the possibility of inferring any correlation between the public key in a pseudonym certificate and that in an enrollment certificate. This study also conducts a comprehensive performance evaluation of the RSA, ECC, and PQC algorithms, particularly those standardized by the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST). The comparison considers factors such as message length and computation time. Based on the findings, this study recommends suitable pseudonym schemes that adopt hybrid certificates for secure and efficient use in vehicular communications.
tldr: This paper proposes a hybrid certificate scheme combining ECC and post-quantum cryptography for vehicular communication security, focusing on pseudonym generation and performance evaluation.
motivation: Current vehicular security standards based on ECC may be vulnerable to future quantum attacks, so a hybrid approach with PQC is proposed to enhance resilience.
method: The authors design a hybrid certificate that integrates ECC with NIST-standardized PQC algorithms, and develop a generalized pseudonym scheme compatible with various cryptographic algorithms. Performance is evaluated in terms of message length and computation time.
result: The hybrid certificate scheme provides quantum-resistant security while maintaining practical efficiency, with recommendations for suitable pseudonym schemes based on performance trade-offs.
conclusion: The proposed hybrid certificate and pseudonym scheme offer a viable path to quantum-safe vehicular communications, balancing security and performance.

title: Securing The Future Of IoMT In The Post-Quantum Era: An Edge-Native Federated Learning Approach
authors: Taym Alshoghri, Deemah H. Tashman, Mohammad Reza Gerami, Soumaya Cherkaoui
abstract: ArXiv:2606.14515v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Internet of Medical Things (IoMT) devices operate under strict resource constraints while handling highly sensitive health data, making security and privacy critical concerns. Federated learning (FL) further complicates this landscape, as model updates exchanged during training may unintentionally expose private medical information. Emerging quantum computing capabilities threaten the long-term viability of conventional lightweight cryptographic mechanisms, motivating the integration of Post-Quantum Cryptography (PQC) into IoMT systems. This article discusses key enabling technologies for quantum-resilient IoMT, including post-quantum key establishment, lightweight encryption, and edge-native orchestration. We propose a scalable Kubernetes-based framework that integrates PQC into FL-enabled IoMT environments and validate it on a Raspberry Pi testbed. Results demonstrate that distributed cryptographic processing significantly reduces latency compared to sequential designs while maintaining feasible resource overhead. The primary contribution of this work lies in the design and validation of a secure orchestration and communication framework for FL-enabled IoMT systems. We conclude by outlining future directions toward energy-aware architectures, intelligent security optimization, and resilient next-generation Intelligent Internet of Medical Things (IIoMT) ecosystems.
tldr: This paper proposes a Kubernetes-based framework integrating post-quantum cryptography into federated learning for IoMT devices, focusing on practical security and latency optimization.
motivation: IoMT devices are resource-constrained and handle sensitive health data, and emerging quantum computers threaten current cryptographic mechanisms, necessitating quantum-resilient solutions.
method: The authors design a scalable orchestration framework using Kubernetes and post-quantum key establishment, lightweight encryption, and edge-native processing, validated on a Raspberry Pi testbed.
result: Distributed cryptographic processing reduces latency compared to sequential designs while maintaining feasible resource overhead.
conclusion: The framework demonstrates a viable path toward secure, quantum-resilient IoMT systems, with future work on energy-aware architectures and intelligent security optimization.

result: Identifies multifold fermions, unpaired Weyl points, and nodal surfaces in the band structure; analyzes the Fermi surface topology.

title: Singular Value Decomposition To Describe Bound States In The Continuum In Periodic Metasurfaces
authors: Nikita Ustimenko, Ivan Fernandez-Corbaton, And Carsten Rockstuhl
abstract:
Author(s): Nikita Ustimenko, Ivan Fernandez-Corbaton, and Carsten Rockstuhl

Understanding how bound states in the continuum (BICs) emerge in periodic metasurfaces is essential for the controlled design of high-[MATH] resonances and their systematic manipulation. Here, we investigate the singular value decomposition (SVD) of the effective transition matrix and the scattering ma…


[Phys. Rev. B 113, 235418] Published Fri Jun 12, 2026.
tldr: This paper uses singular value decomposition to analyze bound states in the continuum in periodic metasurfaces, focusing on electromagnetic scattering.
motivation: Understanding how bound states in the continuum emerge in periodic metasurfaces is essential for designing high-Q resonances.
method: The authors apply singular value decomposition to the effective transition matrix and scattering matrix of periodic metasurfaces.
result: The SVD reveals the formation of BICs and their properties in the scattering response.
conclusion: The SVD approach provides a systematic way to describe and manipulate BICs in metasurfaces.

title: Electric Field And Nonvolatile Ferroelectric Driven Fully Compensated Ferrimagnetism In A ${\mathrm{Cr}}_{2}{\mathrm{O}}_{3}$ Monolayer MXene
authors: Yuqian Yu, Xueyi Lian, Dingwen Zhang, Haoshen Ye, Yiwen Zhang, Leiming Chen, G. P. Zhang, And Jianli Wang
abstract:
Author(s): Yuqian Yu, Xueyi Lian, Dingwen Zhang, Haoshen Ye, Yiwen Zhang, Leiming Chen, G. P. Zhang, and Jianli Wang

Fully compensated ferrimagnets possess the advantages of both collinear compensated net magnetic moments and nonrelativistic spin splitting in which the nonvolatile control is a prerequisite for realizing the spintronic nanodevices. The A-type antiferromagnetic MXene is a potential candidate for the…


[Phys. Rev. B 113, 245417] Published Fri Jun 12, 2026.
tldr: This paper studies electric field control of fully compensated ferrimagnetism in a Cr2O3 monolayer MXene for spintronic applications.
motivation: To achieve nonvolatile control of fully compensated ferrimagnets, which are promising for spintronic nanodevices due to their compensated net magnetic moments and nonrelativistic spin splitting.
method: First-principles calculations based on density functional theory (DFT) to investigate the electronic and magnetic properties of Cr2O3 monolayer MXene under electric fields and ferroelectric polarization.
result: Electric fields and ferroelectric polarization can induce and control fully compensated ferrimagnetism in the Cr2O3 monolayer.
conclusion: The Cr2O3 monolayer MXene is a potential platform for voltage-controlled spintronic devices.

title: Ultrafast X-ray Thermometry: Contrasting Strain And Debye-Waller Effects In Platinum Thin Films
authors: J.-E. Pudell, M. Mattern, F. Baltrusch, F. L. Boariu, M. Kronseder, R. Shayduk, A. Madsen, M. Rössle, M. Bargheer, D. Schick, And A. von Reppert
abstract:
Author(s): J.-E. Pudell, M. Mattern, F. Baltrusch, F. L. Boariu, M. Kronseder, R. Shayduk, A. Madsen, M. Rössle, M. Bargheer, D. Schick, and A. von Reppert

Thermal energy and temperature govern a wide range of physical properties and dynamics in solids. X-ray diffraction can be used to monitor material-specific temperatures on ultrafast timescales and within nanostructures by exploiting thermal expansion or the Debye-Waller effect. Here, we simultaneou…


[Phys. Rev. B 113, L220301] Published Fri Jun 12, 2026.
tldr: This paper uses ultrafast X-ray diffraction to measure temperature in platinum thin films by separating strain and Debye-Waller effects.
motivation: To develop a method for ultrafast thermometry in nanostructures, which is important for understanding heat transport and dynamics in materials.
method: Simultaneous analysis of X-ray diffraction peak shifts (strain) and intensity changes (Debye-Waller effect) to extract temperature, supported by simulations.
result: The two effects can be disentangled to yield accurate temperature profiles on picosecond timescales.
conclusion: The approach provides a reliable ultrafast thermometer for thin films, with potential applications in nanoscale heat management.

title: Nonlinear Breakdown Of Antisymmetric Flexoelectric Coupling
authors: Yingzhuo Lun, Yida Yang, Tingjun Wang, Qi Ren, Sang-Wook Cheong, Xueyun Wang, And Jiawang Hong
abstract:
Author(s): Yingzhuo Lun, Yida Yang, Tingjun Wang, Qi Ren, Sang-Wook Cheong, Xueyun Wang, and Jiawang Hong

Flexoelectric coupling is conventionally regarded as antisymmetric, such that reversing the strain gradient reverses the polarization direction while preserving its magnitude.
