[Phys. Rev. B 113, 214104] Published Thu Jun 11, 2026.
tldr: This paper reports a nonlinear breakdown of antisymmetric flexoelectric coupling in noncentrosymmetric single crystals under large strain gradients.
motivation: Flexoelectric coupling is conventionally antisymmetric; this work investigates deviations from this behavior under large strain gradients.
method: Experimental measurements and theoretical analysis on noncentrosymmetric single crystals subjected to large strain gradients.
result: The antisymmetric coupling breaks down, leading to nonlinear polarization responses.
conclusion: The findings challenge the conventional antisymmetric assumption and have implications for flexoelectric device design.

title: Large Inverse Magnetocaloric Effect Induced By Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya Interaction In Two-dimensional Ferromagnetic Semiconductors
authors: Guangwei Zhai, Chang Niu, Min Li, Xiong Xu, And Hui Wang
abstract:

Two-dimensional magnets have emerged as a promising platform for nanoscale spintronics and solid-state refrigeration. In this work, we investigate the magnetic phase transitions and magnetocaloric properties of monolayer [MATH] [MATH] using density functional …


[Phys. Rev. B 113, 245202] Published Thu Jun 11, 2026.
tldr: This paper studies the magnetocaloric effect in a 2D ferromagnetic semiconductor driven by Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya interaction using DFT.
motivation: To explore the potential of 2D magnets for nanoscale spintronics and solid-state refrigeration.
method: Density functional theory (DFT) calculations to investigate magnetic phase transitions and magnetocaloric properties.
result: A large inverse magnetocaloric effect is induced by the Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya interaction.
conclusion: The findings suggest that 2D ferromagnetic semiconductors with DMI could be promising for magnetocaloric cooling applications.

title: Tunable Optical Spin Hall Effect In An Open Cavity
authors: Yuquan Zhou, Xin Li, Huihua Chen, Song Luo, Hang Zhou, Zhao Xu, Hongming Zhang, Yaofeng Zhu, Xinyue Zhang, Yan Liu, Zheng Lv, Yuxin Duan, Guoxing Lv, Anpeng Li, Haodong Cheng, Jian Ren, Xiao Wang, Long Zhang, And Zhanghai Chen
abstract:
Author(s): Yuquan Zhou, Xin Li, Huihua Chen, Song Luo, Hang Zhou, Zhao Xu, Hongming Zhang, Yaofeng Zhu, Xinyue Zhang, Yan Liu, Zheng Lv, Yuxin Duan, Guoxing Lv, Anpeng Li, Haodong Cheng, Jian Ren, Xiao Wang, Long Zhang, and Zhanghai Chen

The optical spin Hall effect (OSHE), resulting from photonic spin-orbit coupling, has become a pivotal phenomenon in nanophotonics. While a tunable optical spin Hall effect has been achieved in liquid-crystal-based anisotropic microcavities, a more general material-independent and broadband platform…


[Phys. Rev. B 113, 245416] Published Thu Jun 11, 2026.
tldr: This paper demonstrates a tunable optical spin Hall effect in an open cavity, enabling broadband and material-independent control of photonic spin-orbit coupling.
motivation: The optical spin Hall effect is important for nanophotonics, but existing platforms are limited to specific materials like liquid crystals. A more general, tunable platform is desired.
method: The authors use an open cavity structure to achieve tunable spin-orbit coupling, allowing control over the optical spin Hall effect via cavity parameters.
result: They experimentally demonstrate tunable spin splitting and spin-dependent beam shifts, with broadband operation and material independence.
conclusion: The open cavity platform provides a versatile and tunable approach to the optical spin Hall effect, with potential applications in photonic devices.

title: Phonon-mediated Thermal Transport In Two-dimensional ${\mathrm{MoSe}}_{2}$ At Cryogenic Temperatures From Accelerated ab Initio Calculations
authors: Xinyu Zhang, Cheng Shao, And Hua Bao

Author(s): Xinyu Zhang, Cheng Shao, and Hua Bao

Understanding thermal transport in two-dimensional (2D) materials at cryogenic temperatures is essential for emerging low-temperature nanoelectronics, yet remains largely unexplored because of the lack of a predictive theoretical framework. Here, we develop a rigorous, accelerated, mode-resolved fir…


[Phys. Rev. B 113, 214309] Published Wed Jun 10, 2026.
tldr: This paper studies phonon-mediated thermal transport in 2D MoSe2 at cryogenic temperatures using accelerated ab initio calculations.
motivation: Understanding thermal transport in 2D materials at cryogenic temperatures is important for low-temperature nanoelectronics but lacks a predictive theoretical framework.
method: The authors develop a rigorous, accelerated, mode-resolved first-principles approach to compute thermal conductivity.
result: They obtain mode-resolved thermal transport properties of monolayer MoSe2 at cryogenic temperatures.
conclusion: The work provides a theoretical framework for predicting thermal transport in 2D materials at low temperatures, relevant for nanoelectronics.

title: Dynamics And Pinning For Skyrmions In Altermagnets
authors: J. C. Bellizotti Souza, C. J. O. Reichhardt, A. Saxena, And C. Reichhardt
abstract:

We examine the dynamics, Hall angle, and pinning for Néel skyrmions in an altermagnet. Using an atomistic model, we show that skyrmion velocity and Hall angle dependence are anisotropic with respect to the direction of the drive, due to the fourfold symmetry implied by the two sublattices of the alt…


[Phys. Rev. B 113, 224424] Published Wed Jun 10, 2026.
tldr: This paper studies the dynamics and pinning of skyrmions in altermagnets, focusing on anisotropic velocity and Hall angle effects.
motivation: Understanding skyrmion motion in altermagnets is important for potential spintronic applications, but the paper does not connect to quantum information or thermodynamics.
method: The authors use an atomistic model to simulate Néel skyrmions in an altermagnet with two sublattices, analyzing velocity and Hall angle as functions of drive direction.
result: Skyrmion velocity and Hall angle exhibit strong anisotropy due to the fourfold symmetry of the altermagnet, and pinning effects are characterized.
conclusion: The work provides insights into skyrmion dynamics in altermagnets but is purely classical condensed matter physics without quantum information or thermodynamic relevance.

title: Complete Decomposition Of Anomalous Diffusion In Variable Speed Generalized Lévy Walks
authors: Abhijit Bera And Kevin E. Bassler
abstract:
Author(s): Abhijit Bera and Kevin E. Bassler

Variable speed generalized Lévy walks (VGLWs) are a class of spatiotemporally coupled stochastic processes that unify a broad range of previously studied models within a single parametrized framework. Their dynamics consist of discrete random steps, or flights, during which the walker's speed varies…


[Phys. Rev. E 113, 064124] Published Fri Jun 12, 2026.
tldr: This paper presents a complete decomposition of anomalous diffusion in variable speed generalized Lévy walks, a class of stochastic processes.
motivation: To unify and understand a broad range of anomalous diffusion models within a single parametrized framework.
method: The authors analyze variable speed generalized Lévy walks (VGLWs) using a decomposition approach that separates the process into components.
result: They achieve a complete decomposition of the anomalous diffusion behavior, characterizing the contributions of different flight segments.
conclusion: The work provides a unified theoretical framework for anomalous diffusion, but does not connect to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: Chromatic Percolation In Two-dimensional Multitype Particle Systems With Extended-range Homotypic Repulsion
authors: Tingting Yin, Yan Sui, Xueying Yuan, And Xian Kong
abstract:
Author(s): Tingting Yin, Yan Sui, Xueying Yuan, and Xian Kong

Cells in many tissues repel like neighbors over extended ranges, yet standard jamming models ignore this diversity. We introduce chromatic percolation—the percolation of like-type particles driven by extended-range homotypic repulsion in multitype assemblies—and map its relation to mechanical jammin…


[Phys. Rev. E 113, 065412] Published Fri Jun 12, 2026.
tldr: A study of percolation and jamming in multitype particle systems with extended-range homotypic repulsion, using a model called chromatic percolation.
motivation: To understand how extended-range homotypic repulsion affects percolation and mechanical jamming in diverse cell assemblies, which is relevant to tissue biology.
method: The authors introduce chromatic percolation, a percolation model for like-type particles with extended-range repulsion, and analyze it via simulations and theoretical mapping to jamming.
result: They find that extended-range homotypic repulsion can induce chromatic percolation transitions that are correlated with mechanical jamming.
conclusion: The work provides a framework linking percolation and jamming in multitype systems, with implications for understanding tissue mechanics.

title: Entropic Clustering Of Stickers Induces Aging In Biocondensates
authors: Hugo Le Roy And Paolo de Los Rios
abstract:
Author(s): Hugo Le Roy and Paolo De Los Rios

Biomolecular condensates are cellular phase-separated droplets that usually exhibit a viscoelastic mechanical response, a behavior rationalized by modeling the complex molecules that make up a condensate as stickers and spacers, which assemble into a network-like structure. Condensates usually exhib…


[Phys. Rev. E 113, 064405] Published Tue Jun 09, 2026.
tldr: This paper models biomolecular condensates as sticker-spacer networks and shows that entropic clustering of stickers leads to aging behavior.
motivation: Biomolecular condensates exhibit viscoelastic mechanical response, which is not fully understood. The authors aim to explain aging in these systems using a minimal model.
method: The authors develop a theoretical model based on stickers and spacers, where stickers form reversible crosslinks. They analyze the dynamics using a master equation and Monte Carlo simulations.
result: They find that entropic clustering of stickers causes the system to age, with the relaxation time increasing over time, consistent with experimental observations.
conclusion: The model captures the aging behavior of biocondensates, suggesting that entropic effects play a key role in their mechanical properties.

title: Further Testing The Validity Of Generalized Heterogeneous-elasticity Theory For Low-frequency Excitations In Structural Glasses
authors: Walter Schirmacher, Matteo Paoluzzi, Felix Cosmin Mocanu, Dmytro Khomenko, Grzegorz Szamel, Francesco Zamponi, And Giancarlo Ruocco
abstract:

We summarize the salient features of our theory of nonphononic vibrational excitations in glasses [W. Schirmacher et al.,
tldr: This paper tests the validity of generalized heterogeneous-elasticity theory for low-frequency excitations in structural glasses, focusing on nonuniversal scaling of the vibrational density of states.
motivation: Understanding low-frequency vibrational excitations in glasses is important for explaining their thermal and mechanical properties, but the universality of the scaling law is debated.
method: The authors summarize their previous theory and provide further computational evidence by analyzing the nonphononic vibrational density of states in model glasses.
result: They demonstrate nonuniversality of the ω^4 scaling of the nonphononic density of states, supporting their generalized heterogeneous-elasticity theory.
conclusion: The findings confirm that low-frequency excitations in glasses are not universal and depend on microscopic details, validating the proposed theory.

title: Diffusion-driven Pattern Formation In An Opinion Dynamical Network Model
abstract:
Author(s): Tim Mauch and Thilo Gross

The spatial organization of individuals and their interactions in communities are important factors known to preserve diversity in many complex systems. Inspired by metapopulation models from ecology, we study opinion formation using a network-based approach in which nodes represent communities of i…


[Phys. Rev. E 113, 064302] Published Thu Jun 04, 2026.
tldr: This paper studies opinion formation using a network-based metapopulation model, focusing on spatial pattern formation and diversity preservation.
motivation: Understanding how spatial organization and network structure influence opinion diversity in complex social systems.
method: A network model where nodes represent communities with internal dynamics, coupled via migration-like interactions, analyzed using linear stability analysis and numerical simulations.
result: The model exhibits diffusion-driven pattern formation, leading to spatially heterogeneous opinion states that can preserve diversity.
conclusion: Spatial coupling and network topology can sustain opinion diversity, analogous to ecological metapopulation dynamics.

title: Minority Takeover In Majority Dynamics: Searching For Rare Initializations Via The History Passing Algorithm
authors: Marek Jankola, Freya Behrens, Cédric Koller, And Lenka Zdeborová

tldr: This paper studies majority dynamics on random regular graphs, focusing on the minimal bias needed for a minority to take over, using a history passing algorithm.
motivation: Understanding how initial conditions affect global consensus in deterministic majority dynamics on large random graphs.
method: The authors analyze synchronous deterministic majority dynamics on random d-regular graphs and propose a history passing algorithm to search for rare initial configurations that lead to minority takeover.
result: They find that a small bias in the initial configuration can cause the minority to become the majority, and characterize the threshold bias as a function of graph degree.
conclusion: The work provides insights into the sensitivity of majority dynamics to initial conditions, with implications for social dynamics and distributed computing.

title: Free-energy Model Of Ferroelectric Transition In P(VDF-TrFE) Copolymer
authors: Vadim V. Atrazhev, Dmitry V. Dmitriev, And Vadim I. Sultanov

The low-temperature ferroelectric phase is an orthorhombic crystal analogous to the poly(vinylidene difluoride) β-phase, wh…

tldr: Develops a free-energy model for the ferroelectric-to-paraelectric phase transition in P(VDF-TrFE) copolymers.
motivation: To understand the phase transition in a technologically relevant ferroelectric polymer.
method: Constructs a physics-based analytical free-energy model incorporating dipole interactions and chain conformations.
result: The model reproduces the first-order phase transition and predicts the temperature dependence of polarization.
conclusion: The model provides a quantitative description of the ferroelectric transition in P(VDF-TrFE) copolymers.

title: Visualizing Phonon Edge States On Molybdenum Disulfide

tldr: This paper uses HR-TEM image simulations to show that enhanced atomic vibrations near edges of MoS2 are due to localized phonon edge modes.
motivation: Enhanced atomic vibrations observed near edges of 2D materials in HR-TEM were not well understood; the authors aimed to explain this phenomenon.
method: The authors performed HR-TEM image simulations that include correlated atom vibrations to model the effect of phonon edge modes.
result: The simulations account for the observed enhanced vibrations, confirming the presence of localized phonon edge states.
conclusion: Phonon edge modes are responsible for the enhanced atomic vibrations at edges of MoS2, providing insight into edge effects in 2D materials.

title: Dynamical Learning In Deep Asymmetric Recurrent Neural Networks
authors: Davide Badalotti, Carlo Baldassi, Marc Mézard, Mattia Scardecchia, And Riccardo Zecchina

[Phys. Rev. Research 8, 023281] Published Thu Jun 11, 2026.
tldr: This paper studies dynamical learning in asymmetric recurrent neural networks, focusing on the emergence of stable configuration manifolds.
motivation: To understand how asymmetric interactions and self-couplings in recurrent neural networks can lead to complex dynamical behaviors and learning.
method: The authors analyze recurrent neural networks with asymmetric interactions, incorporating self-couplings or sparse excitatory intermodule connections, and study the resulting dynamical properties.
result: They find that such networks develop a densely connected manifold of dynamically accessible stable configurations, which enhances learning and representation capacity.
conclusion: Asymmetric recurrent neural networks with appropriate couplings can exhibit rich dynamics beneficial for learning, with potential implications for understanding neural computation.

title: Observation Of An Amplitudelike Mode In The Excitonic Insulator ${\mathrm{Ta}}_{2}{\mathrm{Pd}}_{3}{\mathrm{Te}}_{5}$
authors: Y.-S. Choi, Dirk Wulferding, Raju Kalaivanan, Rajesh Kumar Ulaganathan, Raman Sankar, And Kwang-Yong Choi

tldr: Observation of an amplitude-like mode in the excitonic insulator Ta2Pd3Te5 using Raman spectroscopy.
motivation: Excitonic insulators are a platform for macroscopic quantum condensation and collective excitations; identifying collective modes is key to understanding their physics.
method: Polarization-resolved Raman spectroscopy was used to identify a symmetry-selective electronic mode in Ta2Pd3Te5.
result: A symmetry-selective electronic mode was observed, interpreted as an amplitude-like mode of the excitonic condensate.
conclusion: The findings provide evidence for collective excitations in excitonic insulators, advancing the understanding of these quantum materials.

title: Reducibility Of Higher-order To Pairwise Interactions: Social Impact Models On Hypergraphs
authors: Jaume Llabrés, Raúl Toral, Maxi San Miguel, And Federico Vázquez
abstract:
Author(s): Jaume Llabrés, Raúl Toral, Maxi San Miguel, and Federico Vázquez

We show that a general class of node-update social impact models with higher-order interactions on hypergraphs can be exactly mapped to an equivalent model with pairwise interactions on a weighted projected network. This mapping preserves the microscopic probabilities of changing the state of the no…


[Phys. Rev. Research 8, 023250] Published Fri Jun 05, 2026.
tldr: This paper shows that a class of social impact models with higher-order interactions on hypergraphs can be exactly reduced to pairwise interactions on a weighted projected network.
motivation: Higher-order interactions are common in social systems but are computationally complex; the authors aim to simplify such models to enable analysis using standard network tools.
method: The authors derive an exact mapping from a general class of node-update social impact models on hypergraphs to an equivalent model with pairwise interactions on a weighted projected network, preserving microscopic transition probabilities.
result: The mapping is proven to be exact for the considered class of models, allowing higher-order dynamics to be studied via pairwise interactions.
conclusion: This reduction simplifies the analysis of social impact models and may be extended to other dynamical processes on hypergraphs.

title: Kinetic Event-chain Algorithm For Active Matter
authors: Nico Schaffrath, Thevashangar Sathiyanesan, Tobias A. Kampmann, And Jan Kierfeld
abstract:

We present a cluster kinetic Monte Carlo algorithm for active matter systems of self-propelled particles with special focus on steric interactions. The kinetic event-chain algorithm is based on the event-chain Monte Carlo method and is applied to active Brownian disks in two dimensions. The algorith…


[Phys. Rev. Research 8, 023252] Published Fri Jun 05, 2026.
tldr: A kinetic Monte Carlo algorithm for simulating active Brownian disks with steric interactions.
motivation: Efficient simulation of active matter systems with many particles and steric interactions is computationally challenging.
method: The kinetic event-chain algorithm extends the event-chain Monte Carlo method to active Brownian disks, enabling cluster moves and handling steric interactions.
result: The algorithm shows improved efficiency over standard methods for dense active matter systems.
conclusion: The kinetic event-chain algorithm provides a useful tool for simulating active matter, but is not directly relevant to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: Multiobjective Tweezers In Scattering Media

Radiation forces and torques enable the manipulation of objects with acoustic and electromagnetic waves. Yet, harnessing them in complex scattering media remains a formidable challenge, especially when multiple objects must be controlled under competing objectives. Here, we demonstrate that sound or…


[Phys. Rev. Research 8, 023254] Published Fri Jun 05, 2026.
tldr: This paper demonstrates multi-objective manipulation of particles using acoustic tweezers in complex scattering media.
motivation: Controlling multiple objects with radiation forces in scattering environments is challenging, especially under competing objectives.
method: The authors use wavefront shaping and optimization algorithms to simultaneously trap and manipulate multiple particles in a scattering medium.
result: They achieve simultaneous trapping and independent control of multiple particles, demonstrating robustness to scattering.
conclusion: Multiobjective tweezers enable advanced manipulation in complex media, with potential applications in biophysics and microfluidics.

title: Three-Dimensional Xy Universality And Nonlinear Magnetic Susceptibility In A Kagome Ice Compound
authors: Kan Zhao, Hao Deng, Hua Chen, Nvsen Ma, Noah Oefele, Jiesen Guo, Xueling Cui, Chen Tang, Matthias J. Gutmann, Thomas Mueller, Yixi Su, Vladimir Hutanu, Changqing Jin, And Philipp Gegenwart
abstract:
Author(s): Kan Zhao, Hao Deng, Hua Chen, Nvsen Ma, Noah Oefele, Jiesen Guo, Xueling Cui, Chen Tang, Matthias J. Gutmann, Thomas Mueller, Yixi Su, Vladimir Hutanu, Changqing Jin, and Philipp Gegenwart

Nonlinear magnetic susceptibility measurements in the kagome spin ice HoAgGe reveal hidden time-reversal symmetry breaking in the ground states, reached via a three-dimensional XY universality class transition.


[Phys. Rev. X 16, 021043] Published Tue May 26, 2026.
tldr: This paper reports nonlinear magnetic susceptibility measurements in a kagome ice compound, revealing a three-dimensional XY universality class transition and hidden time-reversal symmetry breaking.
motivation: To understand the nature of the ground state and phase transition in the kagome spin ice HoAgGe, which exhibits frustration and potential novel magnetic order.
method: Nonlinear magnetic susceptibility measurements were performed on single crystals of HoAgGe, combined with neutron scattering and theoretical modeling.
result: The system undergoes a phase transition belonging to the three-dimensional XY universality class, and the ground state shows hidden time-reversal symmetry breaking.
conclusion: The kagome ice compound HoAgGe provides a realization of three-dimensional XY criticality and reveals subtle symmetry breaking in the ordered state.

title: Robust Orbital-Selective Flat Bands In Layered Transition-Metal Oxyhalides At Room Temperature
authors: Xiangyu Luo, Ludovica Zullo, Sahaj Patel, Dongjin Oh, Willa Mihalyi-Koch, Emma Lian, Jiaruo Li, Qian Song, Asish K. Kundu, Anil Rajapitamahuni, Elio Vescovo, Natalia Olszowska, Rafał Kurleto, Dawid Wutke, Xavier Roy, Giorgio Sangiovanni, And Riccardo Comin
abstract:
Author(s): Xiangyu Luo, Ludovica Zullo, Sahaj Patel, Dongjin Oh, Willa Mihalyi-Koch, Emma Lian, Jiaruo Li, Qian Song, Asish K. Kundu, Anil Rajapitamahuni, Elio Vescovo, Natalia Olszowska, Rafał Kurleto, Dawid Wutke, Xavier Roy, Giorgio Sangiovanni, and Riccardo Comin

Angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy of layered transition-metal oxyhalides reveals intrinsic flat bands that remain stable at room temperature, providing a tunable platform for investigating strongly correlated electron states.

tldr: This paper reports the discovery of robust orbital-selective flat bands in layered transition-metal oxyhalides at room temperature, characterized by angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy.
motivation: Flat bands in strongly correlated materials can host exotic quantum phases, but they are often fragile and only appear at low temperatures. The authors aim to find a material platform with intrinsic flat bands stable at room temperature.
method: The authors synthesize layered transition-metal oxyhalides and use angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy (ARPES) to measure the electronic band structure, revealing flat bands that are orbital-selective and robust up to room temperature.
result: They observe intrinsic flat bands that remain stable at room temperature, with orbital selectivity, providing a tunable platform for studying strongly correlated electron states.
conclusion: Layered transition-metal oxyhalides are promising materials for investigating flat-band physics and strongly correlated phenomena at accessible temperatures.

title: Continuous Thermochemical Sources Of AlF Molecules
authors: Pulkit Kukreja, Priyansh Agarwal, Maximilian Doppelbauer, Jionghao Cai, Xiangyue Liu, Eduardo Padilla, Sebastian Kray, Henrik Haak, Russell Thomas, Stefan Truppe, Boris G Sartakov, Gerard Meijer And Sid Wright
abstract: The AlF molecule, currently subject to laser cooling and trapping efforts, has the advantage that it can be efficiently produced in a thermochemical reaction between sublimated aluminum trifluoride and aluminum metal. Here we present a series of experiments with continuous molecular beam sources of AlF, utilizing this reaction. We demonstrate a compact AlF molecular beam oven whose total far-field brightness is molecules per steradian per second at 923 K, just below the melting temperature of aluminum metal. The continuous output from the oven begins to exceed the peak brightness of a jet-cooled, ablation-based supersonic AlF source for the , level, and we obtain an excellent signal-to-noise ratio with the oven in pulsed laser ionization spectroscopy experiments. By delivering flux from the oven into a cryogenic Ne buffer gas cell, we lower the rotational temperature of the beam to around 30 K and reduce its most probable forward velocity from 600 m s to 200 m s . In addition, we demonstrate that AlF can be made in a simple dispenser package, and observe that molecules thermalize to the laboratory temperature after colliding with vacuum chamber walls of the experiment. The resulting transient AlF vapor may enable direct loading of a molecular magneto-optical trap.
tldr: This paper presents experimental demonstrations of continuous thermochemical sources for producing AlF molecules, focusing on molecular beam brightness and cooling for laser cooling and trapping.
motivation: AlF molecules are promising for laser cooling and trapping, but efficient and continuous sources are needed for advanced experiments.
method: The authors use a thermochemical reaction between sublimated aluminum trifluoride and aluminum metal to produce AlF, and characterize the molecular beam using spectroscopy and buffer gas cooling.
result: They achieve a compact oven with high brightness, continuous output exceeding pulsed sources, and demonstrate rotational cooling to ~30 K using a cryogenic buffer gas cell.
conclusion: Continuous thermochemical sources of AlF are viable and can enable direct loading of magneto-optical traps, advancing molecular quantum science.

title: Distinguishing Near- Versus Off-critical Phase Behaviors Of Intrinsically Disordered Proteins
authors: Gaurav Mitra, Souradeep Ghosh, Kiersten M Ruff, Ruoyao Zhang, Gaurav Chauhan And Rohit V Pappu
abstract: Intrinsically disordered prion-like low complexity domains (PLCDs) drive phase transitions that underlie the biogenesis of many biomolecular condensates. Here, we report results from large-scale Monte Carlo simulations on lattices aided by computations of Binder cumulants and rigorous finite-size scaling. These approaches enable accurate mapping of the critical regime and computations of the full binodal of an archetypal PLCD. This weakly associating polymer undergoes phase separation coupled to percolation. Between the lowest temperature and the critical point, the concentrations along the left arm of the binodal vary by four orders of magnitude. The overlap line intersects the left arm of the binodal well below the critical point. This, taken together with the intersection of the percolation line and the left arm of the binodal, leads to demarcation of the binodal into three regimes. Regime I is farthest from the critical point. Here, the coexisting dilute phase is akin to a gas of dispersed polymers. The dilute arm of the binodal lies above the overlap line in Regimes II and III. Here, the semidilute nature of dilute phases enables clustering of polymers that is enhanced by intermolecular associations. The coexisting dense phases form confined percolated networks in Regimes I and II. In Regime III, which is closest to the critical point, the dense phase becomes unconfined and fragmented, and the system is defined by two interconnected, system-spanning networks. In addition to mapping the critical point accurately, we evaluated methods for identifying the theta temperature. We find that scaling approaches based on assumptions from two-parameter theories for homopolymers yield erroneous estimates of the theta temperature of an archetypal PLCD. Accurate estimation of the theta temperature requires direct calculation of the temperature dependence of the two-body interaction coefficient. We discuss implications for inferring solvent quality from scaling analysis of segmental distances of disordered proteins.
tldr: This paper uses Monte Carlo simulations and finite-size scaling to study phase behavior of intrinsically disordered proteins, focusing on critical vs. off-critical regimes.
motivation: Understanding phase transitions of prion-like low complexity domains is important for biomolecular condensate biogenesis, but the paper is purely biophysical without quantum or information-theoretic aspects.
method: Large-scale Monte Carlo simulations on lattices with Binder cumulants and finite-size scaling to map binodals and percolation lines.
result: The binodal is divided into three regimes based on overlap and percolation lines; scaling approaches from homopolymer theory give erroneous theta temperature estimates.
conclusion: Accurate theta temperature estimation requires direct calculation of the two-body interaction coefficient, with implications for solvent quality inference.

title: Direct Single-shot Imaging Of Time-resolved Terahertz Vector Fields
authors: J. Lafreniere-Greig, J. E. Nkeck, X. Ropagnol, G. Gandubert, Salim Hmidi, O. Brincoveanu, O. -G. Simionescu, E. Abraham, R. Tudor, F. Blanchard
abstract: ArXiv:2606.14011v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We demonstrate direct single-shot retrieval of the full in-plane vector field of broadband terahertz waves using electro-optic sampling. Implemented with a circularly polarized optical probe and polarization-sensitive camera, the method overcomes the projection constraints of conventional electro-optic sampling and enables direct time-domain reconstruction of transverse vector fields without Fourier-domain inversion or sequential polarization analysis. We experimentally validate the approach through spatiotemporal imaging of linear, circular, azimuthal and radial terahertz fields generated by polarization-engineered silicon metamaterials. The measurements reveal ultrafast time-resolved vector-field dynamics inaccessible to conventional scalar detection, including helicoidal field rotation within a single optical cycle and the spatiotemporal evolution of structured polarization topologies. Beyond structured-field imaging, we demonstrate single-scan vector-field spectroscopy through measurements of quartz birefringence and broadband terahertz waveplate performance. More broadly, this work transforms electro-optic sampling from a projection-based measurement into a vector-resolved imaging and spectroscopy platform for structured electromagnetic fields.
tldr: This paper presents a method for direct single-shot imaging of time-resolved terahertz vector fields using electro-optic sampling with a circularly polarized probe and polarization-sensitive camera.
motivation: Conventional electro-optic sampling is projection-based and cannot capture full vector fields in a single shot, limiting the study of structured terahertz fields.
method: The authors use a circularly polarized optical probe and a polarization-sensitive camera to simultaneously measure both orthogonal components of the terahertz field, enabling direct time-domain reconstruction without Fourier inversion.
result: They experimentally validate the technique by imaging linear, circular, azimuthal, and radial terahertz fields from polarization-engineered silicon metamaterials, revealing ultrafast vector-field dynamics and demonstrating single-scan vector-field spectroscopy.
conclusion: This work transforms electro-optic sampling into a vector-resolved imaging and spectroscopy platform for structured electromagnetic fields.

title: Analysis Of A Compact Interferometric Imager
authors: Laurent M. Mugnier, Vincent Michau, Hiyam Debary, Fr\'ed\'eric Cassaing
abstract: ArXiv:2606.14224v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The advent of photonic integrated circuits (PICs) will allow the replacement of the large aperture of an optical telescope by a dense array of small apertures combined interferometically. The light coming from aperture pairs can be combined by a PIC in order to extract interferogram characteristics known as complex visibilities, from which the observed object can then be reconstructed. In such a compact interferometric imager, the optical components dedicated to image formation in a regular telescope are no longer necessary. In particular, such a concept is relevant for space missions where weight and size are critical. In this communication, we study such an instrument concept, focusing on signal-to-noise considerations. We recall the design basis for the field and the spatial resolution, and we show that the spectral resolution must be no less than the field to resolution ratio. Then, we analyze the signal-to-noise ratio of this concept, assuming that each spatial frequency is recorded only once, and compare the signal-to-noise ratio with that of a monolithic telescope. We perform the comparison in Fourier space for an identical number of recorded photons. We show that the noise propagation of the interferometric imager is identical to that of a monolithic telescope that would have a flat Modulation Transfer Function with a level roughly given by the ratio of the small apertures' diameter to the maximum baseline. We conclude that the noise propagation in low and medium spatial frequencies is unfavorable for the interferometric imager.
tldr: This paper analyzes the signal-to-noise ratio of a compact interferometric imager using photonic integrated circuits, comparing it to a monolithic telescope.
motivation: To replace large telescope apertures with dense arrays of small apertures combined interferometrically for space missions where weight and size are critical.
method: The authors derive design basis for field and spatial resolution, show spectral resolution constraints, and compare noise propagation in Fourier space assuming identical photon counts.
result: Noise propagation of the interferometric imager is identical to a monolithic telescope with a flat Modulation Transfer Function at a level given by the ratio of small aperture diameter to maximum baseline.
conclusion: The interferometric imager has unfavorable noise propagation at low and medium spatial frequencies compared to a monolithic telescope.

title: Nodal Degeneration Of Chiral Algebras Ii: Local Structure And Chiral Zhu Algebras
abstract: ArXiv:2606.13986v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Given a vertex algebra [MATH], Zhu constructed an associative algebra [MATH], whose representation theory provides an approximation to the category of [MATH]-modules. We describe a geometric construction of a certain derived associative algebra [MATH] associated to any universal factorization algebra [MATH], whose zeroth homology recovers Zhu's associative algebra in the case where [MATH] is obtained from a vertex algebra. The construction is given by integrating [MATH] over stable configurations parametrized by two-pointed semistable genus zero curves. By a variant of this construction, we obtained a chiral [MATH]-bimodule [MATH] describing the value of a factorization algebra at a nodal point. We show that its zeroth homology recovers the bimodule underlying the mode-transition algebra [MATH] defined by Damiolini, Gibney, and Krashen, which they use to describes a vertex algebra at a node. Finally, the value over a formal smoothing of a node provides a deformation [MATH] of [MATH], whose zeroth homology describes a deformation of the mode-transition algebra in the case of a vertex algebra.
tldr: This paper develops a geometric construction of a derived associative algebra from a universal factorization algebra, recovering Zhu's algebra and mode-transition algebras for vertex algebras.
motivation: To provide a geometric framework for understanding the representation theory of vertex algebras, particularly at nodal points on curves.
method: The construction integrates a factorization algebra over stable configurations parametrized by two-pointed semistable genus zero curves, and studies deformations via formal smoothings of nodes.
result: The zeroth homology of the constructed algebra recovers Zhu's associative algebra and the bimodule underlying the mode-transition algebra of Damiolini, Gibney, and Krashen.
conclusion: The geometric approach yields a deformation of the mode-transition algebra, offering new insights into vertex algebra structures at nodes.

title: Proof And More Variations Of Bellman's Lost-in-a-forest Problem
abstract: ArXiv:2606.13987v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In this paper, based on our previous general formulation and computational solution to Bellman's Lost-in-a-forest Problem, we provide the proof of general solution and obtained more variations and results related to this problem. This paper provides generalized formalized method connecting curve covering, lost-in-the-forest problem, and traveling salesman problem with neighborhoods. We prove the equivalence and convergence. We also provide more results of searching for two lines, connection to Wetzel's unit arc covering problem, variations with closed path, variations in three dimensions, etc. The results include general calculation equations, partial analytical results, and numerical results.
tldr: This paper provides proofs and variations of Bellman's lost-in-a-forest problem, a geometric optimization problem about curve covering and search paths.
motivation: To generalize and prove the solution to Bellman's lost-in-a-forest problem and explore its connections to other covering problems.
method: The authors use formalized methods connecting curve covering, lost-in-the-forest problem, and traveling salesman problem with neighborhoods, proving equivalence and convergence.
result: They provide general calculation equations, partial analytical results, and numerical results for various settings including two lines, Wetzel's problem, closed paths, and three dimensions.
conclusion: The work extends the theoretical understanding of search and covering problems but has no direct connection to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: Theory And Applications Of Convolution-Based Short Time Offset Linear Canonical Transform
authors: Gita Rani Mahato, Manab Kundu, Alit Elsa Xavier
abstract: ArXiv:2606.14102v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In this paper, we introduce a convolution based short time offset linear canonical transform (STOLCT) and investigate its fundamental mathematical properties. Specifically, we establish its continuity, orthogonality relations, inversion formulas, range theorem, and convolution theorem. We further explore several important applications of STOLCT, including the Poisson summation formula, the Paley Wiener criterion, and a sampling theorem. In addition, numerical simulations and graphical analyses are presented to compare signal reconstruction performance under different scenarios. A comparative study between STOLCT and STLCT is conducted with respect to their reconstruction formulas, demonstrating the effectiveness and potential advantages of the proposed transform.
tldr: This paper introduces a convolution-based short time offset linear canonical transform and studies its mathematical properties and signal processing applications.
motivation: To generalize the short time linear canonical transform by incorporating a convolution operation, enabling better signal reconstruction and analysis.
method: The authors define the STOLCT, prove its continuity, orthogonality, inversion, range, and convolution theorems, and derive Poisson summation, Paley-Wiener, and sampling theorems. Numerical simulations compare reconstruction performance.
result: The STOLCT is shown to be a valid transform with desirable mathematical properties, and numerical experiments demonstrate its effectiveness over the standard STLCT in certain scenarios.
conclusion: The proposed transform offers potential advantages for signal processing, but the paper is purely mathematical and unrelated to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: Zhu's Algebra And The $C_2$-algebra Of A Classically Free Vertex Operator Algebra
abstract: ArXiv:2606.14407v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We prove that, for a classically free vertex algebra, the [MATH]-algebra is naturally isomorphic to the associated graded algebra of Zhu's algebra. As an application, we show that non-trivial holomorphic VOAs of CFT type are not classically free. This includes the affine vertex operator algebra of [MATH] at level one, as well as the Moonshine VOA.
tldr: This paper proves an isomorphism between Zhu's algebra and the C2-algebra for classically free vertex algebras, and applies it to show that non-trivial holomorphic VOAs of CFT type are not classically free.
motivation: To understand the structure of vertex operator algebras (VOAs) and their associated graded algebras, particularly for classically free VOAs.
method: Algebraic and categorical methods in vertex algebra theory, constructing isomorphisms between Zhu's algebra and the C2-algebra.
result: The C2-algebra of a classically free vertex algebra is naturally isomorphic to the associated graded algebra of Zhu's algebra. Non-trivial holomorphic VOAs of CFT type, including the affine VOA of E8 at level one and the Moonshine VOA, are not classically free.
conclusion: Classical freeness is a restrictive condition that excludes many important VOAs, providing insight into the structure of holomorphic VOAs.

title: From Phase Semantics To Base-extension Semantics (and Back)
abstract: ArXiv:2606.13855v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Linear logic admits a wide range of semantic presentations reflecting its resource-sensitive notion of consequence. One well-known example is phase semantics: an algebraic semantics in which formulas are interpreted in phase spaces, consisting of a commutative monoid and a fixed subset, with respect to which an orthogonality relation is defined. A rather different and much more recent approach is given by base-extension semantics, which defines validity by inductively extending a provability relation on a base -- a set of inference rules over atomic propositions. We establish an equivalence between the two semantics by first defining bidirectional maps between bases and phase spaces, and then constructing an isomorphism between a phase space (resp. base) and its image under the composition of these maps. As a further contribution, we define the base-extension semantics clauses for the exponentials of linear logic.
tldr: The paper establishes an equivalence between phase semantics and base-extension semantics for linear logic, including clauses for exponentials.
motivation: To bridge two distinct semantic approaches for linear logic, which have different conceptual foundations and applications.
method: Defines bidirectional maps between bases and phase spaces, then constructs an isomorphism between a phase space (or base) and its image under composition of these maps.
result: An equivalence between phase semantics and base-extension semantics is proven, and base-extension semantics is extended to handle the exponentials of linear logic.
conclusion: The two semantics are essentially equivalent, providing a unified perspective on the resource-sensitive semantics of linear logic.

title: Crypto X Ai, Ai X Crypto: A Survey
authors: Sarah Allen, Pranay Anchuri, James Austgen, Maryam Bahrani, Samuel Breckenridge, Aaron Buchwald, Christian Cachin, Andr\'es F\'abrega, Jared Fernandez, James Hsin-Yu Chiang, Marwa Mouallem, Roi Bar-Zur, Neil Desilva, Ittay Eyal, Giulia Fanti, Ari Juels, Andrew Miller, Christian Sillaber, Dani Vilardell, Pramod Viswanath, Wenhao Wang, Matt Weinberg, Sen Yang, Jianzhu Yao, Fan Zhang
abstract: ArXiv:2606.13892v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The intersection of crypto x AI is spawning papers, products, online posts, and companies. All the surrounding buzz, though, obscures what exactly has been done, what the opportunities and challenges are, and what open questions deserve attention. This survey paper asks what AI can do for blockchain-based technologies (broadly construed as "crypto") (crypto x AI), and vice versa (AI x crypto). We systematize existing work, summarize key takeaways, highlight open research questions, and offer a perspective on pervasive industry misconceptions, concluding that AI and crypto are still in the very early stages of meaningful integration.
tldr: A survey of the intersection between AI and blockchain technologies, covering applications and open questions.
motivation: To systematize the growing body of work at the intersection of AI and crypto, clarify opportunities and challenges, and correct industry misconceptions.
method: The authors review existing literature and industry developments, categorize approaches, and summarize key takeaways.
result: The survey finds that AI and crypto are still in early stages of meaningful integration, with many open research questions.
conclusion: AI and crypto have potential synergies but require further research and development for practical integration.

title: An Entropy Potential For Type-Composition Games
authors: Morteza Alimi, Merlin de la Haye, Pascal Lenzner, \v{s}imon Schierreich, Alexander Skopalik, Marcus Wunderlich
abstract: ArXiv:2606.14428v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Potential functions are a key tool in theoretical computer science with applications ranging from the runtime analysis of algorithms and data structures, through the analysis of the expected behavior of random processes and search heuristics, to proving the existence of equilibrium states in strategic games. Typically, proofs that employ potential functions are short, elegant, and easy to verify, yet very powerful. Moreover, potential functions are essential ingredients for constructive proofs, in particular in algorithmic game theory. There, a key question is the existence of equilibrium states, but the most powerful theorem in the field -- Nash's theorem -- is unfortunately non-constructive. For many strategic games, potential functions come to the rescue by enabling constructive proofs that sometimes even yield efficient algorithms for finding equilibria. We add to this by providing a novel class of entropy-inspired log-multinomial potential functions for natural game-theoretic settings where rational agents of different types strategically choose actions to maximize their utility. In particular, we consider utility functions that are based on the fraction of same- and other-type agents taking the same action. We demonstrate the versatility of the new potential function class by presenting simple equilibrium existence proofs for two recent game-theoretic models, for which only involved technical proofs were previously known. Even better, the new potential function class yields efficient algorithms for constructing equilibria for much more general models. Thereby, we positively resolve several open problems.
tldr: This paper introduces entropy-inspired potential functions for type-composition games in algorithmic game theory, with no connection to quantum information or thermodynamics.
motivation: To provide constructive proofs of equilibrium existence in strategic games where agents' utilities depend on the fraction of same- and other-type agents taking the same action.
method: The authors define a novel class of log-multinomial potential functions based on entropy, and apply them to two recent game-theoretic models.
result: The new potential functions yield simple equilibrium existence proofs and efficient algorithms for constructing equilibria, resolving several open problems.
conclusion: The entropy-inspired potential functions are a versatile tool for equilibrium analysis in type-composition games.

title: History Of The Muddy Children Puzzle
abstract: ArXiv:2606.13703v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The Muddy Children Puzzle is a puzzle about knowledge and ignorance that has been inspiring for the development of epistemic logic. Who came up with it first? This is unclear. We trace the origin of the Muddy Children Puzzle through logical and literary publications over the past two centuries. The puzzle inspired a numerous variations such as involving numbers or coloured hats. We also present a novel hats puzzle involving self-reference.
tldr: A historical and literary tracing of the origin and variations of the Muddy Children Puzzle, a classic epistemic logic problem.
motivation: To clarify the unclear origin of the Muddy Children Puzzle and document its evolution through logical and literary publications over two centuries.
method: Historical literature review and logical analysis of puzzle variations, including a novel self-referential hats puzzle.
result: Traces the puzzle's roots to 19th-century publications and presents a new variation involving self-reference.
conclusion: The puzzle's origin remains ambiguous, but its influence on epistemic logic is well-documented; the new variation adds to the family of knowledge puzzles.

method: First-principles calculations based on density functional theory (DFT) to compute defect formation energies and electronic structure.
result: The material is intrinsically n-type, not p-type, due to low formation energy of oxygen vacancies and gallium interstitials.
conclusion: Spinel LiGa5O8 is not suitable as a p-type transparent semiconductor; alternative doping strategies are needed.

motivation: To understand the nonlinear and nonperturbative dynamics of stars orbiting a supermassive black hole, which serves as a test case for statistical closure theories.
method: An iterative scheme based on the Martin–Siggia–Rose formalism is developed to compute dynamical correlation functions.
result: The scheme compares well with numerical simulations, validating the approach.
conclusion: The Martin–Siggia–Rose formalism can be effectively applied to gravitational systems to compute correlation functions beyond perturbation theory.

authors: Zhiyuan Cheng, Chun Liu, Yan Wang, And Hong Liu

Surface-initiated polymerization on anisotropic templates provides a useful framework for exploring polymerization-driven self-assembly under nonequilibrium conditions. tldr: This paper studies species extinctions in large ecological communities using generalized Lotka-Volterra equations, focusing on feasibility and single-parameter scaling.
motivation: Understanding the conditions for species coexistence and the triggers of extinctions is a key problem in ecology.
method: The authors analyze stationary population abundances in multispecies ecosystems modeled by generalized Lotka-Volterra equations.
result: They identify a single-parameter scaling that governs extinctions and assess the feasibility of coexistence.

title: Edwards Thermodynamic Framework Controls Density Segregation In Cyclically Sheared Granular Materials
authors: Haiyang Lu, Houfei Yuan, Shuyang Zhang, Zhikun Zeng, Yi Xing, Jiazhao Xu, Xin Wang, And Yujie Wang

Granular segregation is a widespread phenomenon observed in various industrial applications, geophysical processes, and daily life events. It can be driven by multiple mechanisms, and numerous models have been proposed to elucidate this behavior. However, most of these models are phenomenological an…

tldr: This paper proposes a thermodynamic framework based on Edwards' theory to explain density segregation in cyclically sheared granular materials.
motivation: Granular segregation is common but lacks a unified thermodynamic description; existing models are phenomenological.
method: The authors apply Edwards' statistical mechanics of granular matter, defining a compactivity-like parameter and using simulations or experiments to test predictions.
result: The framework successfully captures density segregation patterns observed in cyclic shear.
conclusion: Edwards' thermodynamics provides a predictive, first-principles approach to granular segregation.

title: Electron Penetration Heating In Turbulent Magnetic Loops Driven By Nonrelativistic Laser-plasma Interaction
authors: Zheng Gong, Sida Cao, Caleb Redshaw, And Matthew R. Edwards

Using particle-in-cell simulations to study nonrelativistic laser pulse propagation in an under-critical plasma, we identify a novel mechanism that occurs during the growth of turbulent magnetic loops: electron penetration heating. The loops have an electromagnetic left-hand chirality distinct from …


[Phys. Rev. E 113, 065205] Published Mon Jun 08, 2026.
tldr: This paper studies electron penetration heating in turbulent magnetic loops driven by nonrelativistic laser-plasma interaction using particle-in-cell simulations.
motivation: To understand a novel heating mechanism in laser-plasma interactions relevant to inertial confinement fusion and astrophysical plasmas.
method: Particle-in-cell simulations of nonrelativistic laser pulse propagation in under-critical plasma.
result: Identified electron penetration heating during growth of turbulent magnetic loops with left-hand chirality.
conclusion: The mechanism may impact energy transport in laser-produced plasmas.

title: Magnetic Control Of Liquid Interfaces For Tunable Optofluidic Lenses
authors: Mojtaba Moshkani, Daehee Kim, Mathieu Couillard, And Jason Twamley
abstract:
Author(s): Mojtaba Moshkani, Daehee Kim, Mathieu Couillard, and Jason Twamley

Liquid lenses offer a versatile route to adaptive optics, but most existing implementations rely on mechanical deformation or high-voltage actuation, which limits scalability and long-term stability. Here, we demonstrate tunable liquid lenses based on magnetic body forces acting on optically transpa…


[Phys. Rev. E 113, 065503] Published Mon Jun 08, 2026.
tldr: This paper demonstrates tunable liquid lenses using magnetic body forces on ferrofluid interfaces, enabling adaptive optics without mechanical parts or high voltage.
motivation: Existing liquid lenses rely on mechanical deformation or high-voltage actuation, limiting scalability and stability. The authors aim to provide a more robust and tunable alternative using magnetic control.
method: They use optically transparent ferrofluids and apply external magnetic fields to deform the liquid interface, creating a tunable lens. The lens shape and focal length are controlled by adjusting the magnetic field strength and configuration.
result: They achieve tunable focal lengths with fast response times and demonstrate stable, reversible lensing without mechanical fatigue or electrical breakdown.
conclusion: Magnetic control of liquid interfaces offers a promising approach for adaptive optics in applications requiring compact, low-power, and reliable tunable lenses.

title: Circular Dichroism In The Photoelectron Angular Distribution Of Achiral Molecules
authors: Christian S. Kern, Xiaosheng Yang, Giovanni Zamborlini, Simone Mearini, Matteo Jugovac, Vitaliy Feyer, Umberto de Giovannini, Angel Rubio, Serguei Soubatch, Michael G. Ramsey, F. Stefan Tautz, And Peter Puschnig
abstract:
Author(s): Christian S. Kern, Xiaosheng Yang, Giovanni Zamborlini, Simone Mearini, Matteo Jugovac, Vitaliy Feyer, Umberto De Giovannini, Angel Rubio, Serguei Soubatch, Michael G. Ramsey, F. Stefan Tautz, and Peter Puschnig

Circular dichroism in the angular distribution (CDAD) is the effect that the angular intensity distribution of photoemitted electrons depends on the handedness of the incident circularly polarized light. The origin of CDAD can be manifold, including intrinsic properties of the system under study, su…


[Phys. Rev. Research 8, 023275] Published Thu Jun 11, 2026.
tldr: This paper studies circular dichroism in photoelectron angular distributions from achiral molecules, a phenomenon in photoemission spectroscopy.
motivation: Understanding the origin of circular dichroism in photoelectron angular distributions (CDAD) from achiral molecules, which can arise from experimental geometry or final-state effects.
method: Combined experimental measurements using angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy (ARPES) with circularly polarized light and theoretical simulations based on one-step photoemission theory.
result: CDAD is observed in achiral molecules and attributed to the experimental geometry and the symmetry of the initial and final states, not molecular chirality.
conclusion: CDAD in achiral systems is a geometric effect that must be accounted for when interpreting photoemission data, but it does not indicate chirality.

result: Analytical expressions for energy loss probability are obtained, showing how nonlocal effects modify the plasmonic response.

title: Membrane-associated Self-assembly For Cellular Decision-making
authors: Samuel L. Foley And Margaret E. Johnson
abstract:

tldr: This paper studies membrane-associated self-assembly for cellular decision-making, a topic in biophysics and systems biology.

authors: Karen Nakanishi, Masaaki Kakoki, Kiyotaka Ohwada, Kenta Kuroda, Kazuki Sumida, Hitoshi Sato, Koji Miyamoto, Taichi Okuda, Shinji Isogami, Keisuke Masuda, Yuya Sakuraba, And Akio Kimura

title: Elastic And Structural Anisotropy In Silica Thin Films For Gravitational-Wave Detectors
authors: Brenda Bracco, Michele Magnozzi, Stefano Colace, Maurizio Canepa, Giulio Favaro, Marco Bazzan, Massimo Granata, David Hofman, Alessandro Di Michele, Laura Silenzi, Gianpietro Cagnoli, Giovanni Carlotti, Paola Sassi, And Silvia Corezzi

Researchers find that silica films in mirror coatings of gravitational-wave detectors have hidden anisotropy that resists standard heat treatment. This discovery informs coating design and deposition and postprocessing strategies aimed at reducing thermal noise.

result: They find hidden anisotropy in silica films that resists standard heat treatment, which has implications for coating design and postprocessing.
conclusion: The discovery informs strategies for reducing thermal noise in gravitational-wave detectors by optimizing coating deposition and annealing processes.

authors: I. Festi, E. Alfinelli, D. Bessas, F. Caporaletti, A. I. Chumakov, M. Moratalla, M. A. Ramos, M. Rodríguez-López, C. Rodríguez-Tinoco, J. Rodríguez-Viejo, And G. Baldi

[Phys. Rev. X 16, 021021] Published Tue Apr 28, 2026.

motivation: Understanding the vibrational properties of glasses is important for their mechanical and thermal behavior, but the connection between glass stability and low-frequency vibrations is not well understood.

title: Subsurface Driven Size-Dependent Elasticity In Nanodiamond
authors: Jiaqi Zhang, Chunmeng Liu, Xing Li, Dongyang Wang, Keke Zhao, Houlin Ji, Yoshifumi Oshima, Shaobo Cheng, And Chongxin Shan

method: The authors use experimental characterization and theoretical modeling to investigate how subsurface structures affect the elastic response of nanodiamond particles.
result: They find that subsurface compliant regions enable significant elastic deformation, leading to size-dependent elasticity that deviates from bulk diamond behavior.
conclusion: The work provides a pathway to tailor the mechanical properties of diamond through subsurface engineering, which could impact nanodevice design.

abstract:

result: The model predicts spontaneous segregation and patterning driven by mechanical forces, consistent with experimental observations.
conclusion: Mechanical forces and hydrodynamic flows are key drivers of chromatin organization, offering a physical basis for nuclear architecture.

title: Radiation Forces And Torques In Optics And Acoustics
authors: Ivan Toftul, Sebastian Golat, Francisco J. Rodríguez-Fortuño, Franco Nori, Yuri Kivshar, And Konstantin Y. Bliokh
abstract:

This review presents a unified perspective of how local energy, momentum, and spin densities in optical and acoustic wave fields induce forces and torques on particles—a topic that has captivated researchers for centuries. Applications discussed include trapping and manipulation of atoms and nanoparticles by light, sorting of biological cells by the combination of acoustics and microfluidics, and pulling forces that draw particles against the direction of wave propagation.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 98, 025002] Published Thu Apr 30, 2026.
tldr: A review of radiation forces and torques in optics and acoustics, focusing on wave-matter interactions and particle manipulation.
motivation: To provide a unified perspective on how local energy, momentum, and spin densities in wave fields induce forces and torques on particles.
method: Review of theoretical and experimental work on optical and acoustic radiation forces, including trapping, sorting, and pulling effects.
result: Summarizes key principles and applications of radiation forces and torques in both optics and acoustics.
conclusion: The field has broad applications in particle manipulation, but the paper does not connect to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: Colloquium: Geospace Pathfinder Science At Arecibo Observatory
authors: J. D. Mathews, M. P. Sulzer, And Shikha Raizada
abstract:
Author(s): J. D. Mathews, M. P. Sulzer, and Shikha Raizada

The Arecibo Observatory housed the largest single-aperture radio telescope for approximately 50 years. A major scientific focus was studying the upper atmosphere; its highly sensitive radar facility, combined with lidars, optical sensors, and satellite-based systems, enabled unprecedented studies of ionospheric physics based on incoherent scattering of radio waves off free electrons. After establishing the fundamental concepts and observables of the incoherent scattering radar technique, this Colloquium reviews key advances obtained with the Arecibo suite of instruments in multiple areas of geospace science, including plasma physics, space weather, lidar studies of atomic metals in the ionosphere, and ionosphere-magnetosphere coupling.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 98, 011005] Published Tue Mar 31, 2026.
tldr: This Colloquium reviews advances in geospace science made using the Arecibo Observatory's radar and lidar instruments, focusing on ionospheric physics and space weather.
motivation: The Arecibo Observatory's unique capabilities for studying the upper atmosphere and ionosphere have led to significant insights, and this review aims to summarize those contributions.
method: The paper reviews the incoherent scatter radar technique and presents results from Arecibo's radar, lidar, and optical instruments, combined with satellite data.
result: Key advances in plasma physics, space weather, metal atom layers, and ionosphere-magnetosphere coupling are discussed.
conclusion: The Arecibo Observatory has been instrumental in advancing geospace science, and its legacy continues through ongoing analysis and future directions.

title: Pressure Effects On Metals, Alloys, And Compounds Of Transplutonium Elements
authors: Tyler W. Hines, Nicholas B. Beck, Kacy N. Mendoza, Joseph M. Sperling, And Thomas E. Albrecht

title: Colloquium: Multimessenger Astronomy With Continuous Gravitational Waves And Future Detectors
abstract:
Author(s): Benjamin J. Owen

The search for continuous gravitational waves from rotating neutron stars represents a key frontier of gravitational-wave astrophysics, with strong connections to electromagnetic astronomy, nuclear astrophysics, and condensed matter physics. This Colloquium discusses the detection prospects for these long-lived yet elusive signals in the upcoming generation of gravitational-wave detectors, emphasizing the importance of simultaneous electromagnetic observations. It also surveys the potential implications of such multimessenger observations for our understanding of the physical and astrophysical processes taking place in the extremely dense environments of their sources.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 98, 011002] Published Tue Mar 10, 2026.
tldr: This Colloquium reviews the prospects for detecting continuous gravitational waves from rotating neutron stars and their multimessenger connections.
motivation: Continuous gravitational waves are a key frontier in gravitational-wave astrophysics, with implications for nuclear astrophysics and condensed matter physics.
method: The paper surveys detection prospects for upcoming gravitational-wave detectors and discusses simultaneous electromagnetic observations.
result: It highlights the importance of multimessenger observations for understanding dense environments in neutron stars.
conclusion: Future detectors will enhance the search for continuous waves, but the paper does not present new results or methods directly relevant to quantum information or thermodynamics.

title: Neutron Stars And The Dense Matter Equation Of State
authors: Katerina Chatziioannou, H. Thankful Cromartie, Stefano Gandolfi, Ingo Tews, David Radice, Andrew W. Steiner, And Anna L. Watts
abstract:
Author(s): Katerina Chatziioannou, H. Thankful Cromartie, Stefano Gandolfi, Ingo Tews, David Radice, Andrew W. Steiner, and Anna L. Watts

Neutron stars, the remnants of supernova explosions, are the densest objects in the Universe. A typical neutron star has a mass between one and two solar masses, and a radius of around 12 km. The density at the center of the star is higher than that in atomic nuclei. As a result, the properties of neutron stars provide important information about the behavior of ordinary matter under extreme compression. In recent years, new information about neutron stars has emerged from two sources. The first is the observation of the gravitational-wave signal from the final inspiral of a coalescing binary neutron star. The second is a careful measurement of the x-ray pulse profile of a spinning neutron star. This review discusses these measurements and summarizes how they constrain masses, radii, and central densities. The results are compared to predictions based on calculations of the nuclear equation of state at densities comparable to that in atomic nuclei, which are then extrapolated to higher density. The review ends with an outlook on future observational opportunities.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 045007] Published Wed Dec 24, 2025.
tldr: A review of neutron star observations and the dense matter equation of state, focusing on gravitational waves and X-ray pulse profiles.
motivation: To understand the behavior of matter at extreme densities, which is key for nuclear physics and astrophysics.
method: Summarizes recent gravitational-wave detections from binary neutron star mergers and X-ray pulse profile measurements, comparing them to theoretical equation of state models.
result: Provides constraints on neutron star masses, radii, and central densities, and compares with nuclear equation of state predictions.
conclusion: Neutron star observations offer unique insights into dense matter, with future observations expected to further refine the equation of state.
