title: A Modern Large-Scale Memory Characterization Laboratory
authors: Ataberk Olgun, Haocong Luo, Ismail Emir Yuksel, F. Nisa Bostanci, A. Giray Yaglikci, Onur Mutlu
abstract: ArXiv:2606.13725v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Real memory chip characterization yields insights into fundamental operational characteristics of modern memory, enabling new mechanisms that improve memory performance, robustness, security, and energy efficiency. We describe our large-scale DRAM characterization laboratory for understanding DRAM. A key building block of this laboratory is DRAM Bender, a versatile and easy-to-use modern DRAM characterization infrastructure. We have updated DRAM Bender to i) introduce support for new types of characterization experiments, ii) expand on its DRAM interface standard support, and iii) make it easier to use at large scale. This paper introduces these updates for the first time. We hope our infrastructure enables the community to discover new problems and solve critical memory scaling issues, enabling the overcoming of the huge memory bottleneck that plagues modern computing systems.
tldr: This paper describes updates to DRAM Bender, an infrastructure for large-scale DRAM characterization, focusing on memory performance, robustness, and energy efficiency.
motivation: Understanding real DRAM chip characteristics is crucial for improving memory performance, robustness, security, and energy efficiency in modern computing systems.
method: The authors extend DRAM Bender with support for new characterization experiments, additional DRAM interface standards, and improved scalability for large-scale use.
result: The updated infrastructure enables more comprehensive and efficient DRAM characterization experiments.
conclusion: The work aims to help the community address critical memory scaling issues and overcome the memory bottleneck in computing.

title: Beyond LoRA: Is Sparsity-Induced Adaptation Better?
authors: Elijah Cadenhead, Cristian Mcgee, Xin Li, El Houcine Bergou, Aritra Dutta
abstract: ArXiv:2606.13767v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Low-rank adaptation (LoRA) and its variants provide a memory- and compute-efficient alternative to full fine-tuning of pre-trained models. However, questions remain about the comparative generalizability of these approaches and how the structural restrictions on low-rank updates preserve effective adaptation performance. We present a historical framing, covering the past (full fine-tuning and original LoRA), the present (different variants of LoRA), and propose simpler, cheaper, parameter-efficient extensions by inducing sparsity within existing LoRA variants: Cheap LoRA (cLA), training a single low-rank factor with the other fixed (deterministically or, in its randomized variant, stochastically), and the chained circulant variant, [MATH]LA. We frame cLA as a structured instance of asymmetric LoRA, serving as a controlled column-subspace restriction of full fine-tuning. We derive information-theoretic generalization error bounds for these variants, marking one of the first endeavors in this area. Empirically, we evaluate 11 fine-tuning methods across 10 pre-trained models and 14 datasets, analyzing the fine-tuned models' performance and generalization using tools such as loss landscapes and spectral analysis. Despite the sensitivity of fine-tuned models to the pre-trained model, datasets, and other factors, our study suggests that restricting LoRA-based PEFT methods' adaptation to a sparse, structured column space remains competitive across tasks with their parameter-matched baselines while reducing up to 10% training time and peak GPU memory up to 15%, even with a na\"ive, non-optimized, sparse implementation. Our theoretical and empirical generalization measures provide a more consistent and principled approach to their cost-effective adaptation than commonly used analytical tools. Overview and code are available at: [URL].
tldr: This paper proposes sparse variants of LoRA for parameter-efficient fine-tuning of large pre-trained models, with theoretical generalization bounds and empirical evaluation.
motivation: To improve the efficiency and generalization of fine-tuning large models by inducing sparsity in low-rank adaptations.
method: Introduces Cheap LoRA (cLA) and chained circulant variants, trains only one low-rank factor, and derives information-theoretic generalization bounds.
result: Sparse structured updates achieve competitive performance with up to 10% training time and 15% peak memory reduction.
conclusion: Sparsity-induced adaptation is a viable alternative to standard LoRA, offering efficiency gains without sacrificing performance.

title: Safety-Contract Graph Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning For Autonomous Network Security Response
authors: Jose Luis Lima de Jesus Silva
abstract: ArXiv:2606.13832v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Autonomous network-security response systems promise to reduce Security Operations Centre (SOC) reaction latency, but reward-only multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) can improve security reward while remaining non-deployable. We present a safety-contract graph MARL framework and instantiate it as ACD[MATH]-GAT (Adaptive Constrained Counterfactual Decisioning with a Graph Attention Network encoder), an architecture that separates simulator observations from reusable operational budgets, constrained optimization, graph state encoding, and counterfactual action screening. We evaluate the method in CAGE Challenge 4, where agents operate under budgets for Mean Time to Recover (MTTR), false-positive response, and firewall change-management disruption. Across the benchmark, every unconstrained method violates the SOC downtime budget in 100% of evaluated episodes, with mean downtime proxy costs of 311-430 against a budget of 50. This complements prior CAGE Challenge 4 findings by showing that reward-only learning lacks operational discipline. Constrained MAPPO-GAT (C-MAPPO-GAT) isolates Lagrangian operational-cost control and budget-aware screening, while ACD[MATH]-GAT adds budget context, CVaR tail-risk estimation, opponent-belief state, and Graph Counterfactual Risk Propagation (G-CRP). The replicated comparison includes three 200-episode seeds for IPPO, MAPPO-GAT, C-MAPPO-GAT, and ACD[MATH]-GAT. C-MAPPO-GAT reduces downtime violation from 100% to 0.3% and mean downtime cost from 355.4 to 15.5 relative to MAPPO-GAT. ACD[MATH]-GAT reduces mean downtime cost to 48.2 with a 13.8% violation rate, placing it on the safety-contract frontier rather than at the most conservative compliance point. Topology-seed and coupled adaptive Red-process stress tests preserve this contrast and show lower worst adaptive degradation for safety-constrained policies than reward-only MAPPO-GAT.
tldr: This paper presents a safety-contract graph multi-agent reinforcement learning framework for autonomous network security response, evaluated on the CAGE Challenge 4 benchmark.
motivation: Reward-only multi-agent reinforcement learning for network security can improve security metrics but often violates operational constraints like downtime budgets, making it non-deployable.
method: The authors propose ACD[MATH]-GAT, which combines constrained optimization, graph attention network encoding, counterfactual action screening, and CVaR tail-risk estimation to enforce safety contracts.
result: Constrained methods (C-MAPPO-GAT and ACD[MATH]-GAT) significantly reduce downtime budget violations compared to unconstrained baselines, with C-MAPPO-GAT achieving 0.3% violation rate and mean downtime cost of 15.5 vs. 355.4 for MAPPO-GAT.
conclusion: Safety-constrained MARL with explicit budget awareness and risk estimation is essential for deployable autonomous network security response.

title: Bayesian-Calibrated Detection Of Hallucinated Package Imports In AI-Assisted Code
authors: Lom M. Hillah (newco Partners, Paris, France, Sorbonne Universit\'e, CNRS, LIP6, Paris, France), Jean-Marc Richard (newco Partners, Paris, France), Ryan Hasnaoui
abstract: ArXiv:2606.13918v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We present a Bayesian calibration layer for slopsquat detectors -- those that flag hallucinated package imports in code produced by large language models (LLMs). Where existing pipelines emit binary decisions (flag / do-not-flag), our layer emits a Beta-posterior probability per detection, derived from a 3-category epistemic taxonomy that explicitly classifies each prior as empirically calibrated, constructively argued, or engineering-judgement-traced. Beyond the primary 200/404 registry channel, the calibrated layer exploits PyPI metadata signals -- package age, release count, author descriptor, summary -- to surface registered-but-suspicious packages that a binary registry detector misses, which is the realistic post-LLM-emission attacker regime. The resulting risk-aware primitive is directly consumable by downstream CI gates and supports principled threshold decisions across detection rules. We evaluate the calibration on a merged corpus of 1,734 Python snippets -- a stratified 189-prompt BigCodeBench slice plus a 100-prompt niche-library stress-test set, generated across a six-model panel spanning four cloud models (Claude-Sonnet-4.6, Mistral-Large, DeepSeek-v4-pro, DeepSeek-R1) and two local open-weight code models (Mistral Codestral, Meta CodeLlama). Against a re-implemented binary baseline inspired by Mahmud et al. -- which shares its registry oracle with our ground truth and therefore serves as a degenerate upper bound rather than a genuine competitor -- the calibrated layer reproduces the strict-registry detections and introduces well-calibrated additional flags on the metadata channel. We assess detector asymmetry with a McNemar paired test and calibration with both a flagged-subset Expected Calibration Error and a strictly proper full-corpus Brier score.
tldr: This paper presents a Bayesian calibration layer for detecting hallucinated package imports in AI-generated code, focusing on software supply chain security.
motivation: LLM-generated code often contains hallucinated package imports that can lead to security vulnerabilities; existing binary detectors miss suspicious packages that are actually registered.
method: The authors develop a Bayesian calibration layer that outputs a Beta-posterior probability per detection, using a 3-category epistemic taxonomy and PyPI metadata signals to flag registered-but-suspicious packages.
result: The calibrated layer reproduces strict-registry detections and introduces well-calibrated additional flags on the metadata channel, evaluated on a corpus of 1,734 Python snippets.
conclusion: The approach provides a risk-aware primitive for downstream CI gates, enabling principled threshold decisions across detection rules.

title: Harbor: Heading Analysis And Reconstruction From Behavioral Observation And Radar
authors: Joao P. A. Dantas, Paulo F. Silva Filho, Jelton A. Cunha, Gabriel Dietzsch
abstract: ArXiv:2606.14006v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Maritime situational awareness often relies on Automatic Identification System (AIS) transmissions to track vessel movements. However, in operational or conflict scenarios, these data may be unavailable due to signal loss, deliberate deactivation, or intentional spoofing. In such conditions, synthetic aperture radar (SAR) imagery becomes a critical sensing alternative for wide-area maritime monitoring, despite providing only static scene snapshots. This work introduces HARBOR (Heading Analysis and Reconstruction from Behavioral Observation and Radar), a complete pipeline for transforming a single SAR image into predictive motion information without requiring any auxiliary data source at inference time. The method begins with SAR image preprocessing to enhance and segment vessel candidates, followed by automatic detection, size-based classification, and heading estimation using skeleton geometry and local intensity patterns. AIS data are used exclusively during an offline calibration phase to derive vessel-type-dependent motion parameters, which are then applied to generate probabilistic heatmaps of candidate future vessel positions. A case study using real COSMO-SkyMed SAR imagery demonstrates the pipeline on a maritime scene in southern Brazil, showing its ability to extract motion tendencies and generate probabilistic projections of vessel positions in data-denied environments.
tldr: This paper presents a pipeline for vessel heading estimation and motion prediction from single SAR images without AIS data at inference.
motivation: Maritime situational awareness is hindered when AIS data is unavailable due to signal loss or spoofing; SAR imagery offers an alternative but only provides static snapshots.
method: The pipeline preprocesses SAR images to detect and classify vessels, estimates heading using skeleton geometry and intensity patterns, and uses offline-calibrated motion parameters to generate probabilistic future position heatmaps.
result: A case study with COSMO-SkyMed SAR imagery demonstrates the ability to extract motion tendencies and produce probabilistic projections of vessel positions in data-denied environments.
conclusion: The method enables predictive motion information from a single SAR image, aiding maritime monitoring when AIS data is absent.

motivation: To understand and control the formation of microjets from laser-driven shock waves in droplets, relevant for industrial applications like EUV light sources.
method: Experimental: two laser pulses create interfering shock waves in a tin microdroplet, and high-speed imaging captures the resulting jet dynamics.
result: Controlled interference of shock waves enables tuning of jet velocity and direction, achieving high-speed microjets.
conclusion: The technique offers a method to precisely control microdroplet jetting, with potential for improving EUV lithography sources.

title: Sea-surface Retention Effect Shapes Ocean Microplastic Fibers
abstract:
Author(s): Andrea Mazzino and Giuseppe Suaria

Microfibers contaminate the global ocean, but their impact depends on length-dependent residence at the air-sea interface. In the submillimeter range, the sea surface exhibits a surface-enrichment signature: The long-to-short fiber ratio is higher at the interface than a few meters below (about 5 m)…


[Phys. Rev. Research 8, 023283] Published Thu Jun 11, 2026.
tldr: This paper studies the length-dependent retention of microplastic fibers at the sea surface, finding that longer fibers are enriched at the air-sea interface compared to subsurface waters.
motivation: Microplastic fibers are a major pollutant in the ocean, but their vertical distribution and residence time at the sea surface are poorly understood, which affects estimates of their environmental impact.
method: The authors combine field measurements of fiber length distributions at the sea surface and at 5 m depth with a theoretical model of turbulent mixing and buoyancy to explain the observed surface enrichment of longer fibers.
result: The sea surface shows a higher ratio of long to short fibers than subsurface waters, and this enrichment is quantitatively captured by a model that accounts for the balance between turbulent diffusion and fiber rise velocity.
conclusion: The sea surface acts as a selective retention layer for longer microplastic fibers, which has implications for their transport, degradation, and ecological effects.

title: Experimental Demonstration Of Dephasing Reduction In An Optically Guided Laser-plasma Accelerator
authors: Ronan Lahaye, Igor A. Andriyash, Julien Gautier, Olena Kononenko, Adrien Leblanc, Jean-Philippe Goddet, Amar Tafzi, And Cédric Thaury
abstract:
Author(s): Ronan Lahaye, Igor A. Andriyash, Julien Gautier, Olena Kononenko, Adrien Leblanc, Jean-Philippe Goddet, Amar Tafzi, and Cédric Thaury

Laser-plasma accelerators offer a compact means of producing high-energy electron beams, but their performance is fundamentally limited by dephasing between the accelerated electrons and the plasma wave. To overcome this limitation, we investigate the combination of plasma density tapering and optic…


[Phys. Rev. Research 8, 023274] Published Wed Jun 10, 2026.
tldr: This paper demonstrates dephasing reduction in a laser-plasma accelerator using plasma density tapering and optical guiding.
motivation: Laser-plasma accelerators are limited by dephasing between electrons and the plasma wave; overcoming this is crucial for improving electron beam energy and quality.
method: The authors combine plasma density tapering with optical guiding to extend the acceleration length and reduce dephasing, and experimentally characterize the resulting electron beams.
result: They observe a significant reduction in dephasing, leading to higher energy electron beams compared to standard configurations.
conclusion: The technique effectively mitigates dephasing, advancing the performance of laser-plasma accelerators.

title: Generation Of Attosecond Pulses From Relativistic Oscillating Plasma Gratings
authors: Hao-Jie Zhang, Bo-Yuan Li, Xiang-Yan An, Rong Huang, Zheng-Ming Sheng, Feng Liu, And Min Chen
abstract:
Author(s): Hao-Jie Zhang, Bo-Yuan Li, Xiang-Yan An, Rong Huang, Zheng-Ming Sheng, Feng Liu, and Min Chen

We propose a scheme to generate two isolated attosecond pulses at controllable angles through the interaction between relativistic laser pulses and a solid target. Two [MATH]-polarized laser pulses with certain frequency chirps are employed to drive oscillating plasma gratings (OPGs) on the target surf…


[Phys. Rev. Research 8, 023261] Published Mon Jun 08, 2026.
tldr: This paper proposes a scheme to generate attosecond pulses using relativistic oscillating plasma gratings driven by chirped laser pulses.
motivation: Attosecond pulse generation is important for ultrafast science, and the authors aim to produce isolated pulses at controllable angles.
method: Two chirped laser pulses interact with a solid target to create oscillating plasma gratings, which reflect the pulses into attosecond bursts.
result: The scheme yields two isolated attosecond pulses with controllable emission angles.
conclusion: The proposed method offers a new way to generate attosecond pulses with potential applications in ultrafast spectroscopy.

title: Unified Model For Full-stage Shear Thickening Via Surface Chemistry And Friction
authors: Kang Wang, Bing Liu, Quan Liu, Huaxia Deng, And Xinglong Gong
abstract:
Author(s): Kang Wang, Bing Liu, Quan Liu, Huaxia Deng, and Xinglong Gong

Shear thickening fluid exhibits complex properties in a wide range of external conditions, leading to the significance for probing its state-transition property at the molecular level. Here, we propose a constitutive model that unifies the three rheological stages of shear thinning, shear thickening…


[Phys. Rev. Research 8, 023263] Published Mon Jun 08, 2026.
tldr: This paper proposes a constitutive model for shear thickening fluids based on surface chemistry and friction, unifying three rheological stages.
motivation: Shear thickening fluids exhibit complex state transitions under varying conditions, and understanding the molecular-level mechanisms is important for applications.
method: The authors develop a constitutive model that incorporates surface chemistry and friction effects to describe shear thinning, shear thickening, and subsequent thinning.
result: The model successfully unifies the three rheological stages and matches experimental data.
conclusion: The work provides a comprehensive framework for understanding shear thickening behavior, with potential implications for material design.

title: Inhibitory Synaptic Timescales Drive Oscillatory Regime Transitions In Recurrent Excitatory-inhibitory Networks
authors: Siamak Kheiri, Saeed Taghavi, Matjaž Perc, And Alireza Valizadeh
abstract:
Author(s): Siamak Kheiri, Saeed Taghavi, Matjaž Perc, and Alireza Valizadeh

In recurrent cortical networks, inhibitory kinetics are often assumed to tune oscillation frequency continuously. Using a recurrent excitatory-inhibitory (E-I) model with fixed excitatory synaptic dynamics, we systematically vary inhibitory decay time constants and show instead that inhibitory times…


[Phys. Rev. Research 8, 023251] Published Fri Jun 05, 2026.
tldr: This paper studies how inhibitory synaptic timescales drive oscillatory regime transitions in recurrent excitatory-inhibitory networks, a topic in computational neuroscience.
motivation: Understanding how inhibitory kinetics affect oscillation frequency and regime transitions in cortical networks.
method: Systematic variation of inhibitory decay time constants in a recurrent E-I model with fixed excitatory dynamics.
result: Inhibitory timescales can drive transitions between oscillatory regimes, not just tune frequency continuously.
conclusion: Inhibitory kinetics play a critical role in shaping network oscillations beyond simple frequency tuning.

title: Super-resonance: Breaking The Bandwidth Limit Of Resonant Modes And Its Application To Flow Control
authors: Adam R. Harris, Armin Kianfar, David Roca, Daniel Yago, Christoph Brehm, And Mahmoud I. Hussein
abstract:
Author(s): Adam R. Harris, Armin Kianfar, David Roca, Daniel Yago, Christoph Brehm, and Mahmoud I. Hussein

Super-resonance maintains a broadband out-of-phase response well beyond the characteristic bandwidth of conventional resonance, enabling broadband flow stabilization among other applications.


[Phys. Rev. X 16, 021045] Published Thu May 28, 2026.
tldr: This paper introduces super-resonance, a phenomenon that breaks the bandwidth limit of resonant modes, and applies it to flow control.
motivation: Conventional resonance has a limited bandwidth, which restricts applications like flow stabilization. The authors aim to overcome this limitation.
method: The authors theoretically and experimentally demonstrate super-resonance, achieving a broadband out-of-phase response beyond the characteristic bandwidth of conventional resonance.
result: Super-resonance maintains a broadband out-of-phase response, enabling broadband flow stabilization among other applications.
conclusion: Super-resonance provides a new paradigm for resonant systems, with potential applications in flow control and beyond.

title: Erratum: Opposite Effects Of The Rotational And Translational Energy On The Rates Of Ion-Molecule Reactions Near 0 K: The ${\mathrm{D}}_{2}^{+}+{\mathrm{NH}}_{3}$ And ${\mathrm{D}}_{2}^{+}+{\mathrm{ND}}_{3}$ Reactions [Phys. Rev. X 14, 011034 (2024)]
authors: Raphaël Hahn, David Schlander, Valentina Zhelyazkova, And Frédéric Merkt
abstract:
Author(s): Raphaël Hahn, David Schlander, Valentina Zhelyazkova, and Frédéric Merkt
[Phys. Rev. X 16, 029901] Published Wed May 20, 2026.
tldr: This is an erratum correcting a previous paper on ion-molecule reaction rates at low temperatures, unrelated to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.
motivation: The original paper studied rotational and translational energy effects on ion-molecule reactions near 0 K; the erratum corrects errors in that work.
method: The erratum likely corrects experimental or theoretical details from the original study.
result: The erratum provides corrected data or interpretations for the D2+ + NH3 and D2+ + ND3 reactions.
conclusion: The corrected results refine understanding of low-temperature ion-molecule reaction dynamics.

title: Stretching Theory Of Hookean Metashells
abstract:
Author(s): Luca Giomi

A continuum theory that describes how mechanical metamaterials deform on surfaces takes the form of the Schrödinger equation and provides a different path for materials design.


[Phys. Rev. X 16, 021035] Published Thu May 14, 2026.
tldr: A continuum theory for mechanical metamaterials on surfaces is formulated, resembling the Schrödinger equation.
motivation: To develop a theoretical framework for designing mechanical metamaterials that deform on curved surfaces.
method: The author derives a continuum theory that maps the deformation of Hookean metashells to a Schrödinger-like equation.
result: The theory provides a new mathematical description for metashell deformation, enabling novel material design.
conclusion: The work offers a different path for materials design by linking mechanics to quantum-like equations.

title: Using Folded Proteins As Mechanically Well-Defined Units To Understand Fatigue Fracture In Hydrogels: Bridging Single Molecule And Bulk Studies
authors: Liang Dong, Puyu Cao, Huiyan Chen, Yu Zhang, Ying Li, Bin Chen, Yi Cao, And Hai Lei
abstract:
Author(s): Liang Dong, Puyu Cao, Huiyan Chen, Yu Zhang, Ying Li, Bin Chen, Yi Cao, and Hai Lei

A force-response model helps understand fatigue behavior and provides a design strategy for fatigue resistant hydrogels and soft materials.


[Phys. Rev. X 16, 021031] Published Mon May 11, 2026.
tldr: This paper studies fatigue fracture in hydrogels using folded proteins as mechanically well-defined units, bridging single-molecule and bulk experiments.
motivation: Understanding fatigue fracture in soft materials is crucial for designing durable hydrogels, but the molecular mechanisms are poorly understood.
method: The authors use folded proteins as model units to probe mechanical failure at the molecular level and connect single-molecule force spectroscopy with bulk mechanical testing.
result: They develop a force-response model that explains fatigue behavior and provides design principles for fatigue-resistant hydrogels.
conclusion: The work offers a strategy to engineer hydrogels with improved fatigue resistance by controlling molecular-level mechanical properties.

title: Hydroplasticity Of Nanocrystal Films Induced By Mesopore Change
authors: Siyuan Liu, Yonggui Wang, Yu Yin, Xintong Meng, Zhen Lang, And Kai Zhang
abstract:
Author(s): Siyuan Liu, Yonggui Wang, Yu Yin, Xintong Meng, Zhen Lang, and Kai Zhang

A vapor training process allows for improved plasticity and better shaping of wood-derived films.


[Phys. Rev. X 16, 021026] Published Tue May 05, 2026.
tldr: This paper studies the hydroplasticity of nanocrystal films induced by mesopore change, focusing on wood-derived films and vapor training.
motivation: To improve the plasticity and shaping of wood-derived films for practical applications.
method: A vapor training process is used to induce mesopore changes in nanocrystal films.
result: The vapor training process improves plasticity and enables better shaping of the films.
conclusion: The method offers a way to enhance the mechanical properties of wood-derived films.

title: Cell Bulging And Extrusion In A Three-Dimensional Bubbly Vertex Model For Curved Epithelial Sheets
authors: Oliver M. Drozdowski, Büşra Kocameşe-Tamgac𝚤, Kim E. Boonekamp, Michael Boutros, And Ulrich S. Schwarz
abstract:
Author(s): Oliver M. Drozdowski, Büşra Kocameşe-Tamgac𝚤, Kim E. Boonekamp, Michael Boutros, and Ulrich S. Schwarz

Cells at topological defects in curved epithelial sheets experience mechanical forces that facilitate extrusion.


[Phys. Rev. X 16, 021023] Published Thu Apr 30, 2026.
tldr: This paper studies cell bulging and extrusion in curved epithelial sheets using a three-dimensional bubbly vertex model.
motivation: Understanding mechanical forces at topological defects in curved epithelial tissues is important for developmental biology and disease.
method: A three-dimensional bubbly vertex model is developed to simulate curved epithelial sheets and analyze cell shape changes and extrusion.
result: The model shows that cells at topological defects experience mechanical forces that facilitate extrusion, and the curvature of the sheet modulates this process.
conclusion: The bubbly vertex model captures key features of cell behavior in curved epithelia, providing insights into tissue mechanics and morphogenesis.

title: Seeing New Depths: Three-Dimensional Flow Of A Free-Swimming Alga
authors: Gregorius Pradipta, Wanho Lee, van Tran, Kyle Welch, Santosh K. Sankar, Yongsam Kim, Satish Kumar, Xin Yong, Jiarong Hong, Sookkyung Lim, And Xiang Cheng
abstract:
Author(s): Gregorius Pradipta, Wanho Lee, Van Tran, Kyle Welch, Santosh K. Sankar, Yongsam Kim, Satish Kumar, Xin Yong, Jiarong Hong, Sookkyung Lim, and Xiang Cheng

Experimental three-dimensional measurements of the flow field around a free-swimming microalga reveal that microscopic organisms generate unexpected low-Reynolds-number flow phenomena, expanding our understanding of microhydrodynamics with profound biological implications for microbial motility and physiology.


[Phys. Rev. X 16, 021019] Published Fri Apr 24, 2026.
tldr: This paper presents experimental 3D measurements of the flow field around a free-swimming microalga, revealing unexpected low-Reynolds-number flow phenomena.
motivation: Understanding microhydrodynamics of swimming microorganisms is important for biology and fluid dynamics, but the paper does not connect to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.
method: Experimental three-dimensional flow measurements around a free-swimming alga using advanced imaging techniques.
result: Discovery of unexpected flow structures at low Reynolds numbers that expand understanding of microhydrodynamics.
conclusion: The findings have implications for microbial motility and physiology but are unrelated to the user's research interests.

title: Boosting The Thermoelectric Performance Of $α$-MgAgSb Through Phase-Transition-Induced Self-Doping
authors: Kaiwei Guo, Tianyu Wang, Zhen Fan, Lunhua He, Fuhong Chen, Yi Wang, Qi Zhao, Jiawei Yang, Hangtian Zhu, Jun Li, Te-Huan Liu, And Huaizhou Zhao
abstract:
Author(s): Kaiwei Guo, Tianyu Wang, Zhen Fan, Lunhua He, Fuhong Chen, Yi Wang, Qi Zhao, Jiawei Yang, Hangtian Zhu, Jun Li, Te-Huan Liu, and Huaizhou Zhao

A doping-free approach is able to boost thermoelectric performance, providing an attractive route for developing waste heat recovery technologies.


[Phys. Rev. X 16, 021011] Published Fri Apr 10, 2026.
tldr: This paper presents a doping-free method to enhance thermoelectric performance of α-MgAgSb via phase-transition-induced self-doping.
motivation: Thermoelectric materials can convert waste heat into electricity, but traditional doping methods have limitations. A doping-free approach could simplify fabrication and improve performance.
method: The authors induce a phase transition in α-MgAgSb to create self-doping, and characterize the resulting thermoelectric properties.
result: The self-doping significantly boosts the thermoelectric figure of merit (ZT) compared to conventionally doped samples.
conclusion: Phase-transition-induced self-doping is an effective strategy for enhancing thermoelectric performance without external dopants.

title: Fundamentals Of Vacuum Breakdown In High-gradient Accelerator Structures
authors: Walter Wuensch, Sergio Calatroni, Flyura Djurabekova, Andreas Kyritsakis, And Yinon Ashkenazy
abstract:
Author(s): Walter Wuensch, Sergio Calatroni, Flyura Djurabekova, Andreas Kyritsakis, and Yinon Ashkenazy

Vacuum breakdown or arcing happens when a very strong electric field causes a metal surface in a vacuum to suddenly form plasma, allowing large electrical currents to flow. Breakdown can damage particle accelerators, fusion reactors, satellites, and x-ray devices, though it is useful in technologies like plasma thrusters. Scientists have studied this unpredictable and fast phenomenon for over a century. Recent advances in experiments and computer simulations now provide a coherent mechanistic picture: tiny surface defects, electrical stress, heat, and emitted particles interact in complex ways to trigger breakdowns. These insights could improve high-power technologies and make advanced accelerators more reliable and efficient.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 98, 025004] Published Fri Jun 05, 2026.
tldr: This paper reviews the physics of vacuum breakdown in high-gradient accelerator structures, focusing on surface defects, electrical stress, and plasma formation.
motivation: Vacuum breakdown limits the performance of particle accelerators and other high-voltage devices; understanding its mechanism is crucial for improving reliability and efficiency.
method: The authors synthesize recent experimental observations and computer simulations to build a coherent mechanistic picture of the breakdown process.
result: A unified model emerges where tiny surface defects, electrical stress, heat, and emitted particles interact to trigger breakdowns.
conclusion: These insights can guide the design of more robust accelerator structures and other high-power technologies.

title: Colloquium: Hadron Production In Open-charm Meson Pairs At ${e}^{+}{e}^{−}$ Colliders
authors: Xiongfei Wang, Xiang Liu, And Yuanning Gao
abstract:
Author(s): Xiongfei Wang, Xiang Liu, and Yuanning Gao

Hadron spectroscopy is a frontier of particle physics; searching for new hadrons is crucial for validating the theory of strong interaction (QCD). Investigating how charmonium, a bound state of charm and anticharm quarks, decays and searching for new charmoniumlike states yield valuable insights into strong interaction mechanisms, including quark confinement and gluon binding. Hadrons produced at e− collisions decaying to open-charm meson pairs are a primary source of experimental information for these investigations. This Colloquium reviews current progress from BARBAR, Belle, CLEO-c, and BESIII experiments. As BESIII accumulates high-precision data, it has emerged as the leading facility for measuring hadron production in charm-meson pair systems, and recent advances are highlighted.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 98, 021001] Published Fri Apr 03, 2026.
tldr: A review of hadron production in open-charm meson pairs at e+e- colliders, focusing on charmonium spectroscopy and QCD.
motivation: To understand strong interaction mechanisms such as quark confinement and gluon binding through charmonium decays and searches for new hadrons.
method: Review of experimental results from BaBar, Belle, CLEO-c, and BESIII on hadron production in e+e- collisions decaying to open-charm meson pairs.
result: Summarizes current progress and highlights recent advances from BESIII as the leading facility for such measurements.
conclusion: Hadron spectroscopy in charm systems provides crucial tests of QCD and continues to yield new insights.

title: Editorial: A Tribute To The Arecibo Observatory
authors: Véronique van Elewyck And Dietrich Belitz
abstract:
Author(s): Véronique Van Elewyck and Dietrich Belitz

Three Colloquia honor the Arecibo Observatory’s legacy, exploring its revolutionary impact on planetary radar studies, radio astronomy, and geospace science.

[Rev. Mod. Phys. 98, 010001] Published Tue Mar 31, 2026.
tldr: An editorial tribute to the Arecibo Observatory, summarizing its impact on planetary radar, radio astronomy, and geospace science.
motivation: To honor the legacy of the Arecibo Observatory and its contributions to various scientific fields.
method: The paper is an editorial that reviews the observatory's achievements through three colloquia.
result: Highlights the revolutionary impact of Arecibo on planetary radar studies, radio astronomy, and geospace science.
conclusion: The Arecibo Observatory has left a lasting legacy in multiple areas of science.

title: Colloquium: Planetary Radar At The Arecibo Observatory
authors: Michael C. Nolan, Lynn M. Carter, And Edgard G. Rivera-Valentín
abstract:
Author(s): Michael C. Nolan, Lynn M. Carter, and Edgard G. Rivera-Valentín

For more than two decades, the planetary radar installed at the Arecibo Telescope was the most sensitive instrument of its kind, harnessing the penetrating power of radio waves to perform observations of the (sub)surface of planets, moons, and asteroids in the Solar System—providing a unique perspective on those bodies that helped to drive in situ exploration. This Colloquium presents an overview of the scientific legacy of the Arecibo radar system, focusing on the period posterior to the Gregorian Update in the late 1990s until the unexpected demise of the telescope in 2020. After recalling the basics of planetary radar techniques, it reviews key Arecibo observations of Mercury, Venus, Mars, our Moon, and the Saturn system, and highlights its essential role in the characterization of a large sample of near-Earth asteroids and comets.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 98, 011003] Published Tue Mar 31, 2026.
tldr: A review of planetary radar observations at Arecibo Observatory, focusing on Solar System bodies.
motivation: To summarize the scientific legacy of the Arecibo planetary radar system after its upgrade.
method: Review of radar techniques and key observations of planets, moons, and asteroids.
result: Highlights unique subsurface and surface insights from radar data that complemented in situ missions.
conclusion: Arecibo radar was a uniquely powerful tool for planetary science, and its loss leaves a gap.

title: Colloquium: Radio Astronomy With The Arecibo 305-m Telescope: In Contemporaneous Context
abstract:
Author(s): Tapasi Ghosh and Chris Salter

The Arecibo Observatory, inaugurated in 1963 as the world’s largest single-dish radio telescope, remained at the forefront of astronomy and atmospheric science for more than five decades, until its catastrophic collapse in December 2020. This Colloquium focuses on Arecibo’s enduring legacy in radio astronomy, offering a historical perspective that emphasizes how successive major upgrades of the telescope continuously expanded its observational capabilities and scientific impact. It presents Arecibo’s most influential contributions in topics as diverse as pulsar studies, the mapping of neutral hydrogen (HI) in the Milky Way and other galaxies, the characterization of the interstellar medium, the imaging of extragalactic radio sources with very long baseline interferometry (VLBI), the search for extraterrestrial intelligence (SETI), and being a major contributor to the first-ever detection of a stochastic gravitational-wave background.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 98, 011004] Published Tue Mar 31, 2026.
tldr: A historical review of the Arecibo radio telescope's contributions to radio astronomy and atmospheric science.
motivation: To document the legacy of the Arecibo Observatory and its scientific impact over five decades.
method: Historical narrative and summary of key scientific results from Arecibo's upgrades and observations.
result: Highlights Arecibo's major contributions to pulsar studies, HI mapping, VLBI, SETI, and gravitational-wave detection.
conclusion: Arecibo was a transformative facility in radio astronomy, and its loss is significant for the field.

title: Colloquium: Convection-cloud Chambers: Experiment And Theory
authors: Steven Krueger And Raymond A. Shaw
abstract:
Author(s): Steven Krueger and Raymond A. Shaw

In warm clouds, drops grow into raindrops through both condensation and collision coalescence, but the observed rapid transition between these mechanisms remains difficult to theoretically explain. The convection-cloud chamber, which reproduces key phenomena such as turbulent fluctuations in droplet concentrations and supersaturation under controlled laboratory conditions, offers a promising approach to addressing this long-standing bottleneck in understanding in cloud physics. This Colloquium reviews the physics underlying the precipitation bottleneck, examines how convection-cloud chambers capture the essential processes, and synthesizes insights from experiments, theory, and computational models that bridge laboratory and atmospheric scales.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 98, 011001] Published Wed Feb 04, 2026.
tldr: This paper reviews convection-cloud chambers as a laboratory tool to study the precipitation bottleneck in warm clouds.
motivation: The rapid transition from condensation to collision-coalescence in warm clouds is poorly understood; controlled experiments are needed.
method: The authors review experimental, theoretical, and computational studies of convection-cloud chambers that reproduce key cloud processes.
result: Convection-cloud chambers can generate turbulent fluctuations in droplet concentrations and supersaturation, bridging laboratory and atmospheric scales.
conclusion: These chambers offer a promising approach to resolving the precipitation bottleneck in cloud physics.

title: Colloquium: Gravitational Waves From Neutrino-driven Core Collapse Supernovae
abstract:
Author(s): A. Mezzacappa and M. Zanolin

The observation of a core collapse supernova explosion of (near-)Galactic origin would constitute a landmark, once-in-a-century event for multimessenger astronomy, eagerly awaited by observers and modelers alike. The detection of gravitational waves, along with photons and neutrinos, from such an event would provide unique insights into the supernova central engine and the physics of the newly forming neutron star. This Colloquium presents the latest progress in core collapse supernova modeling and the associated gravitational wave signal predictions. It also provides an overview of the specific methods of detection and physical parameter estimation that can be implemented for such signals in ground-based laser interferometers, in the context of multimessenger research strategies.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 041002] Published Tue Dec 30, 2025.
tldr: This Colloquium reviews gravitational wave signals from core collapse supernovae and their detection in multimessenger astronomy.
motivation: Core collapse supernovae are rare events that provide unique insights into stellar physics and neutron star formation; detecting gravitational waves alongside photons and neutrinos would enable multimessenger studies.
method: The paper summarizes recent progress in supernova modeling and gravitational wave signal predictions, and discusses detection methods and parameter estimation for ground-based laser interferometers.
result: It presents the latest predictions for gravitational wave signatures from neutrino-driven core collapse supernovae and outlines strategies for multimessenger observation.
conclusion: A Galactic supernova would be a landmark event for multimessenger astronomy, and ongoing detector improvements and modeling efforts are crucial for maximizing scientific return.

title: Colloquium: The Cosmic Dipole Anomaly
authors: Nathan Secrest, Sebastian von Hausegger, Mohamed Rameez, Roya Mohayaee, And Subir Sarkar
abstract:
Author(s): Nathan Secrest, Sebastian von Hausegger, Mohamed Rameez, Roya Mohayaee, and Subir Sarkar

The cosmological principle, which states that the Universe must be statistically isotropic and homogeneous on large scales, is a foundational principle of the standard model of cosmology, known as lambda cold dark matter (ΛCDM). The validity of this principle can be tested by assessing the compatibility of a dipole anisotropy in the large-scale distribution of matter with the dipole observed in the cosmic microwave background, interpreted in the ΛCDM model as due to our local peculiar motion. This Colloquium describes the methodology for such a test and presents its outcome based on the analysis of recent large catalogs of radio galaxies and quasars, revealing a significant inconsistency between the two dipoles. The authors review these recent findings, as well as potential biases, systematic issues, and alternate interpretations, and discuss how this anomaly could challenge the standard description of our Universe based on the ΛCDM model.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 041001] Published Thu Dec 11, 2025.
tldr: This paper reviews the cosmic dipole anomaly, a cosmological observation that challenges the standard ΛCDM model.
motivation: To test the cosmological principle by comparing the dipole in the large-scale matter distribution with the CMB dipole.
method: Analysis of radio galaxy and quasar catalogs to measure the matter dipole and compare it to the CMB dipole.
result: A significant inconsistency is found between the two dipoles, suggesting a possible violation of the cosmological principle.
conclusion: The anomaly may indicate new physics beyond ΛCDM or unknown systematic biases.

title: Astrophysical Tests Of Dark Matter Self-interactions
authors: Susmita Adhikari, Arka Banerjee, Kimberly K. Boddy, Francis-Yan Cyr-Racine, Harry Desmond, Cora Dvorkin, Bhuvnesh Jain, Felix Kahlhoefer, Manoj Kaplinghat, Anna Nierenberg, Annika H. G. Peter, Andrew Robertson, Jeremy Sakstein, And Jesús Zavala
abstract:
Author(s): Susmita Adhikari, Arka Banerjee, Kimberly K. Boddy, Francis-Yan Cyr-Racine, Harry Desmond, Cora Dvorkin, Bhuvnesh Jain, Felix Kahlhoefer, Manoj Kaplinghat, Anna Nierenberg, Annika H. G. Peter, Andrew Robertson, Jeremy Sakstein, and Jesús Zavala

Dark sectors, involving new particles that couple very weakly to the standard model ones, play an important role in current model-building efforts in particle physics, as they allow, for example, for new dark matter production and interaction mechanisms. This review focuses on self-interacting dark matter scenarios, their implications on the dynamics and distribution of dark matter halos in the Universe, and the related astrophysical tests and observations, from galaxies to large-scale structures. It is embedded in the framework of the Novel Probes Project, a forum connecting observers and theorists involved in the study of astrophysical tests of dark-sector interactions.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 045004] Published Mon Dec 08, 2025.
tldr: This paper reviews astrophysical tests of dark matter self-interactions, focusing on dark sector models and their effects on dark matter halos.
motivation: To understand the nature of dark matter and test self-interacting dark matter models using astrophysical observations.
method: Review of theoretical models and observational constraints from galaxies to large-scale structures, including simulations and data comparisons.
result: Summarizes current constraints on dark matter self-interaction cross-sections and outlines future observational prospects.
conclusion: Self-interacting dark matter remains a viable candidate, but more precise astrophysical tests are needed to distinguish it from other models.

title: Prospects For Supersymmetry At High-Luminosity Lhc
authors: Howard Baer, Vernon Barger, Jessica Bolich, Juhi Dutta, Dakotah Martinez, Shadman Salam, Dibyashree Sengupta, And Kairui Zhang
abstract:
Author(s): Howard Baer, Vernon Barger, Jessica Bolich, Juhi Dutta, Dakotah Martinez, Shadman Salam, Dibyashree Sengupta, and Kairui Zhang

Supersymmetry remains one of the leading candidates for physics beyond the standard model, offering a compelling framework to address the hierarchy of scales. Its theoretical appeal has inspired decades of intensive model building and experimental searches. Recent results have placed stringent bounds on the supersymmetric parameter space, sharpening the focus on the remaining viable models. This review surveys the current status and outlook for supersymmetry in light of experimental constraints and recent theoretical developments, and presents projections for the discovery potential of the High-Luminosity Large Hadron Collider across multiple search channels and a variety of well-motivated scenarios.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 045001] Published Fri Oct 17, 2025.
tldr: This paper reviews the prospects for supersymmetry at the High-Luminosity LHC, focusing on experimental searches and model constraints.
motivation: Supersymmetry is a leading candidate for beyond-Standard-Model physics, and the HL-LHC offers new discovery potential.
method: The paper surveys current experimental constraints and theoretical developments, and projects discovery potential across multiple search channels.
result: Stringent bounds have been placed on supersymmetric parameter space, narrowing viable models.
conclusion: The HL-LHC may discover supersymmetry if it exists in certain well-motivated scenarios, but no new results are presented.

title: Solar Fusion Iii: New Data And Theory For Hydrogen-burning Stars
abstract:
Author(s): B. Acharya et al.

Approximately 90% of the stars in the Milky Way are on the main sequence, fusing hydrogen into helium through a network of nuclear reactions. This includes the nearest star, our Sun. A precise understanding of hydrogen burning is crucial to predicting its luminosity, neutrino production, and helioseismology. This review describes the theoretical and experimental work of the last decade that has advanced our understanding of the nuclear physics of hydrogen burning. It describes the plasma and atomic physics that influences the solar environment in which the nuclear reactions take place, as well as the diagnostics probes—including solar neutrinos and helioseismology—that allow us to test our resulting model of the solar interior.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 035002] Published Thu Sep 04, 2025.
tldr: This paper reviews nuclear physics of hydrogen burning in stars, focusing on solar fusion reactions and their astrophysical implications.
motivation: Understanding hydrogen burning is crucial for predicting stellar properties like luminosity, neutrino production, and helioseismology.
method: The paper reviews theoretical models and experimental data from the last decade on nuclear reaction rates, plasma physics, and atomic effects in the solar interior.
result: It summarizes advances in nuclear reaction cross sections, plasma screening, and their impact on solar models, as well as comparisons with neutrino and helioseismic observations.
conclusion: The updated understanding of hydrogen burning improves solar model predictions but does not resolve all discrepancies, motivating further experimental and theoretical work.

title: Gas Bubble Dynamics
abstract:
Author(s): Dominique Legendre and Roberto Zenit

The motion of gas bubbles in liquids plays a vital role in numerous natural, industrial, and everyday phenomena. Unlike solid particles, gas bubbles are nearly weightless and highly responsive to forces from the surrounding fluid. Their dynamics are affected by added mass acceleration and deformable surfaces, and also by interactions with turbulent flows, other bubbles, and walls, with liquid rheology and surfactants further influencing their behavior. This review examines the intricate behavior of noncondensable gas bubbles, highlighting key advances over the past 20 years. Key topics include turbulence, non-Newtonian fluids, and electrolytes, offering insights to enhance modeling and guide future research in two-phase flow systems.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 025001] Published Thu Apr 17, 2025.
tldr: A review of gas bubble dynamics in liquids, covering turbulence, non-Newtonian fluids, and surfactants.
motivation: Gas bubbles are important in many natural and industrial processes, but their dynamics are complex due to deformability and interactions.
method: The paper reviews experimental, theoretical, and numerical advances over the past 20 years.
result: Key advances include understanding of bubble behavior in turbulent flows, non-Newtonian liquids, and the role of surfactants.
conclusion: The review provides insights to enhance modeling and guide future research in two-phase flow systems.

title: Self-aligning Polar Active Matter
authors: Paul Baconnier, Olivier Dauchot, Vincent Démery, Gustavo Düring, Silke Henkes, Cristián Huepe, And Amir Shee
abstract:
Author(s): Paul Baconnier, Olivier Dauchot, Vincent Démery, Gustavo Düring, Silke Henkes, Cristián Huepe, and Amir Shee

What if active units could align–or even antialign–their orientation with their own velocity? This intriguing self-alignment property unlocks a spectrum of fascinating behaviors, from single self-propelled particles orbiting in harmonic traps to transformative collective phenomena like synchronized motion in dense or solid elastic assemblies. Unlike systems where units simply mimic their neighbors, self-alignment fundamentally reshapes how motion emerges, paving the way for groundbreaking discoveries in biology, smart materials, and robotics. This review uncovers the hidden power of self-alignment in active systems, introduces a unified mathematical and conceptual framework, explores existing models of self-alignment, and highlights its transformative impact on the study and real-world applications of active systems.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 015007] Published Thu Mar 20, 2025.
tldr: A review of self-alignment in polar active matter, focusing on collective motion in biological and soft matter systems.
motivation: To understand how self-alignment of active units with their velocity leads to novel collective behaviors, with applications in biology, smart materials, and robotics.
method: The paper reviews existing models and experiments on self-alignment in active matter, presenting a unified mathematical framework.
result: Self-alignment enables phenomena such as orbiting in traps and synchronized motion in dense assemblies, distinct from neighbor-based alignment.
conclusion: Self-alignment is a key mechanism in active matter that can be harnessed for designing new materials and robotic systems.

The buckling of a material surface subject to compression or growth is a ubiquitous phenomenon, arising in materials science contexts such as the swelling of gels as well as in biological contexts such as morphogenesis and embryogenesis. title: Kovacs-like Memory Effect In Strain Stiffening Collagen Networks
authors: Maitri Mandal And Sayantan Majumdar Abhishek Ghadai
abstract: Materials driven far from equilibrium can encode memories of past deformations through long-lived structural reorganizations. Such memory effects-reflecting parameters such as deformation direction, magnitude, and duration have been widely explored in soft amorphous solids. Here, we report a Kovacs-like memory effect manifested as a non-monotonic stress relaxation in vitro biopolymer networks formed by type-I collagen, an essential component of the mammalian extracellular matrix. Using shear rheology combined with in-situ optical imaging, we find that this memory effect emerges exclusively in the nonlinear strain-stiffening regime, and persists over a much broader range of strain amplitudes than previously reported for other viscoelastic amorphous materials. Furthermore, we uncover a strong correlation between the memory response and the development of negative normal stresses and associated strain fields, highlighting the unique nonequilibrium mechanics underlying memory formation in biopolymer networks.
tldr: This paper reports a Kovacs-like memory effect in strain-stiffening collagen networks, focusing on non-equilibrium mechanics of biopolymer networks.
motivation: To understand memory effects in soft amorphous solids and extend them to biopolymer networks, which are relevant to biological tissues.
method: Shear rheology combined with in-situ optical imaging to measure stress relaxation and normal stresses in collagen networks under nonlinear strain-stiffening conditions.
result: A non-monotonic stress relaxation (Kovacs-like memory) is observed exclusively in the nonlinear regime, correlated with negative normal stresses and strain fields.
conclusion: The memory effect in collagen networks arises from unique nonequilibrium mechanics distinct from other amorphous materials, with implications for biological tissue mechanics.

SignificanceGeneral anesthetics are small, lipophilic molecules that interact with a wide array of proteins through low-affinity binding. Despite their promiscuity, these interactions exhibit clear structural specificity, driven by the physicochemical ...
tldr: This paper studies how general anesthetics interact with proteins, revealing functional group-specific biases in binding, which is unrelated to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.
motivation: General anesthetics are promiscuous but structurally specific in protein binding; understanding these biases is important for drug design and safety.
method: The authors performed interactome-wide docking simulations of general anesthetics against a large set of protein targets, analyzing binding affinities and structural preferences.
result: They identified clear functional group-specific biases in anesthetic-protein interactions, showing that certain chemical moieties preferentially bind to specific protein families.
conclusion: The study provides a systematic map of anesthetic-protein interactions, highlighting the need to account for probe reliability in drug discovery.
